results.title: Abandoned Popcorn Time apps had to be disabled to prevent a zombie army
results.author: Stevie Bonifield
results.content:
Remember Popcorn Time, the app that served as an easy-to-use front end for streaming torrents of movies and TV shows? Development of the MPAA’s least-favorite app of the 2010s has been abandoned for years, but the “Netflix of Piracy” software is still installed on millions of devices that are just waiting to join a bot army. Researchers at Eye Security found the updater for a Popcorn Time fork called “Time4Popcorn” still running on tons of Windows, macOS, and Android devices located around the world, phoning home to now-abandoned web domains over unencrypted HTTP and running an outdated, insecure version of Chrome.
Abandoned Popcorn Time apps had to be disabled to prevent a zombie army
What old and vulnerable software might be running on your PC right now?
Eye Security’s Niels Teusink says the updater could have been used to install and run basically any kind of software with full privileges, easily enabling someone to create a botnet just by taking over one of the domains, using a man-in-the-middle attack to target specific devices, or perform surveillance by identifying the machines running the software.
Their solution was to register one of the domains and use it to send their own update that instructed the updater to disable itself. Despite ethical concerns about the fix, the researchers say their only alternative “was to do nothing,” pointing out, “The update process wasn’t doing anything functional anyway, it was only creating risk for users.”
Eye Security said on Windows devices, their update “simply stops and disables the service via the Service Control Manager” without deleting any files or anything else. On macOS, it uses a shell script to execute a command that blocks the update process from starting. They didn’t address the software on Android devices, where installing the update would still require actual user interaction first.
They had to tweak their update after it was uploaded to VirusTotal, causing security programs to flag it as malware and block it while leaving the vulnerable updater running. It’s unclear exactly how many devices were at risk, but Eye Security says it “sent out over 2 million update downloads” by March, when they stopped sending the update and transferred the domains they used to the Shadowserver Foundation, a web security non-profit.
results.summary:
Security researchers have neutralized a massive botnet risk by hijacking abandoned domains associated with the pirated streaming application Popcorn Time to remotely disable the software’s vulnerable update mechanism.

### Key Points
- Eye Security discovered that the "Time4Popcorn" fork remained active on millions of Windows, macOS, and Android devices worldwide.
- The software’s unencrypted update process allowed attackers to execute arbitrary code with full system privileges on infected machines.
- Researchers registered abandoned domains to push a benign update that disabled the insecure service on Windows and macOS systems.
- Over 2 million update downloads were distributed by March before the domains were transferred to the non-profit Shadowserver Foundation.
- The security team bypassed potential malware flags from antivirus software to ensure the disabling script could reach affected devices.

### Why it Matters
This incident highlights the significant security risks posed by abandoned software that continues to communicate with expired or hijacked web domains. Users should audit their devices for legacy applications to prevent them from being exploited as part of a global botnet or surveillance network.

results.title: Windows 11 could get an alternative to Recall, but AI skeptics aren't fans
results.author: Darren Allan
results.content:
- Windows 11 has an alternative take on Recall in testing
- It's an app called the 'Context Vault' offering a similar supercharged search experience
- In this case, though, you have to manually add content to the vault – there's no automatic regular screenshotting of the activity on your PC
Hate the idea of Recall in Windows 11? You wouldn't be alone, so Microsoft is trying a new spin on the idea of an AI-powered supercharged search which is a lot more limited than Recall – although the initial reaction has still been rather negative.
Windows Latest discovered that Microsoft is working on Project Pantheon, the current name of which is the 'Context Vault', and rather than being built into Windows 11 like Recall, this has to be installed from the Microsoft Store.
This isn't just an optional feature, then, it's an app you have to actively seek out, and it works quite differently to Recall in that it doesn't automatically take regular screenshots (snapshots) of the activity on your PC.
Instead, you must manually add the files or content you want to use with the Context Vault, so its AI powers can then make use of them.
To what end? Similar to Recall, you can ask the AI questions about the contents of the vault, or get it to organize material, planning the likes of a summer trip (the example Windows Latest gives) from documents, images, web pages, or even clipboard text saved to the vault.
Note that the app isn't yet officially available, and not listed in the Microsoft Store as such, but Windows Latest managed to find it nonetheless.
Context Vault doesn't necessarily need a Copilot+ PC – or a powerful local NPU, in other words, as it can leverage cloud-based AI – and you can give third-party AI like Claude access to the content in your vault, too, we're told. There's even a panel that tracks your AI token usage in the current build of the vault.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Bear in mind that this is still an early version of the feature, and it sounds pretty wonky right now. It's not clear if this app is something Microsoft will definitely carry forward to a release version for Windows 11, as ever with functionality in testing.
Analysis: is a retake on Recall going to fly?
On the one hand, the full user control over what content Context Vault can access compared to Recall could be a big selling point. On the other hand, using the cloud for running the AI processes is obviously more of a privacy concern (although you don't have to go that route to be fair).
Windows Latest has been led to believe that Microsoft is considering other ways to make the Context Vault more secure, including encryption and per-app access controls, as well as requiring a Windows Hello login for access (as Recall does) to protect the vault from possible local attackers jumping on your device.
As noted at the outset, the reaction to this idea in testing is generally skeptical, and many folks simply see it as 'yet more AI' that Microsoft is cramming into Windows 11 (although it isn't actually confirmed this is coming to the OS, of course).
As one Redditor puts it, this is a classic case of "solving [a] problem [that] doesn't exist."
Another agrees: "Yeah, Microsoft can't even be creative in thinking up something even marginally useful in an extremely far fetched scenario. Literally never in my life felt the need or wanted a tool like Recall or this equally s****y version of it. This problem was solved circa 2000 with bookmarks and Word/Excel documents. Not whatever convoluted trash this is."
In fairness, others are more positive, and there are Recall users out there. One commenter on the same thread says: "I use Recall all the time, it has been a gamechanger for me, I just wish it synced between my devices so I could look up something on my desktop I saw on my tablet."
The one thing that seems clear enough is that the anti-Recall folks aren't going to be swayed by a different take on the same concept, even one that sports a pretty radical change.
The kind of people this might persuade are those who most likely won't be drawn to comment on this idea in testing one way or another. I think it's certainly an alternative that's worth trying for Microsoft, provided it's implemented in a secure enough manner, of course.

### Key Points
- Context Vault functions as an optional Microsoft Store app rather than an integrated system feature like the controversial Recall tool.

results.title: Your guide to voting in New York's 2026 elections for governor and Congress
results.author: Walter Wuthmann, Jon Campbell, Brigid Bergin
results.content:
Election Day is Nov. 3, and it’s time to choose New York’s next governor, attorney general, and congressmembers.
Will voters give Gov. Kathy Hochul a second full term in office? Or will they replace her with Bruce Blakeman, the Republican Nassau County executive with close ties to President Donald Trump? Will Attorney General Letitia James retain her role as the state’s top law enforcement official? And how will New York City voters decide on a series of ballot questions championed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani?
As you wait in line to cast your ballot, here’s a rundown of the candidates, ballot questions and other information.
How and when to vote in NYC
If you want to vote in person, you can find your polling site at vote.nyc.
But you’ll need to remember these key dates:
Oct. 24: In-person early voting begins. Find your early polling site here. Note that hours differ by day, so check the schedule before you go vote. This is also the last day for new voter registration, either online or in-person at your poll site.
Nov. 1: Early voting ends.
Nov. 2: Last day to apply in-person for a mail or absentee ballot at your county’s Board of Elections office.
Nov. 3: Election Day. Polls are open 6 a.m. to 9 p.m. Find your polling site here. (It’s likely different from your early-voting site). Mail-in ballots must be postmarked by Nov. 3.
New York’s candidates for governor
Kathy Hochul, Democrat (incumbent)
Policy priorities: Universal childcare and building more housing. Enacted a moratorium on large data centers. Sent utility rebate checks of up to $200.
Resume: Became the state’s first female governor in 2021 after Andrew Cuomo's resignation. Previously served as lieutenant governor, U.S. representative and Erie County clerk.
Quote: “ Your family is my fight.”
Bruce Blakeman, Republican
Policy priorities: Cutting income taxes and lowering utility bills. Opposes sanctuary policies that restrict the state’s cooperation with Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Opposes data center moratorium.
Resume: First elected Nassau County executive in 2021. Previously served as Hempstead town councilmember and Port Authority commissioner.
Quote: “We can’t afford four more years of Kathy Hochul.”
New York’s candidates for attorney general
Letitia James, Democrat (incumbent)
Policy priorities: Crackdown on illegal firearms and ghost guns, protecting immigrants’ legal rights, and going after predatory lenders and mortgage providers. Has sued the Trump administration over 50 times.
Resume: Attorney general since 2019. Previously served as New York City's public advocate, making her the first Black woman to win and hold citywide office, and a New York City Councilmember representing parts of Brooklyn.
Quote: “No one is above the law, not even the President.”
Saritha Komatireddy, Republican
Policy priorities: More prosecution of street crime, like shoplifting and drug trafficking. Audit and investigate homeless shelters. Investigate waste, fraud and abuse in the public and private sectors.
Resume: Former assistant U.S. attorney in Brooklyn, where she helped prosecute leaders of Al-Qaeda, Islamic State, and Mexican drug cartels. Former chief of staff of the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration under the Biden administration.
Quote: “Public safety is not optional. It’s time for accountability, action and real change.”
New York’s candidates for state comptroller
Tom DiNapoli, Democrat (incumbent)
Policy priorities: Transition fund investments to net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2040. Audit every school district in the state on a rotating cycle. Grew the pension fund to its historic high of $291 billion.
Resume: Second longest-serving comptroller in state history, first elected to the position in 2007. Former state assemblymember representing Nassau County.
Quote: “Transparency is essential so New Yorkers can hold their government and elected officials accountable.”
Joseph Hernandez, Republican
Policy priorities: Aggressively audit state agencies, public authorities and programs. Review state contracts. Create a $10 billion “Empire Opportunity Fund” to invest in emerging businesses and industries, similar to a sovereign wealth fund.
Resume: Longtime Wall Street investor, currently the founder and senior managing partner of Blue Water Venture Partners. Cuban refugee who fled the country at age 7.
Quote: “The fraud and abuse in New York is out of control.”
NYC ballot questions
Voters will find five questions on the back of their ballot. You can read our full breakdown of every question here.
The commission that wrote the proposals says they would:
- Streamline the approval process for pedestrian ramps, benches and sidewalk cafés.
- Modernize city contracting to expand opportunities for small businesses and nonprofit organizations.
- Accelerate road safety projects and the activation of underutilized city property.
- Simplify the building permitting process.
- Require contributions to the rainy day fund to strengthen long-term fiscal resilience.
Congressional races
17th District, Northern Westchester County and the Hudson Valley
Mike Lawler, Republican (incumbent)
Policy priorities: Led battle to expand the state and local tax deduction. Opposes sanctuary policies. Supports reopening Indian Point nuclear plant.
Resume: First elected to the House in 2022. Previously served in the state Assembly.
Quote: “ I'm proud of the fact that I've been rated among the most bipartisan and effective members of Congress.”
Cait Conley, Democrat
Policy priorities: Supports a public option for health insurance, banning congressmembers from trading stocks and creating a path to citizenship for undocumented immigrants living in the United States.
Resume: Former director for counterterrorism on the National Security Council under President Joe Biden. Army officer who served in Iraq and Afghanistan.
Quote: “You deserve better. You deserve a patriot, not a puppet.”
3rd District, Northeast Queens and parts of Nassau and Suffolk counties
Tom Suozzi, Democrat (incumbent)
Policy priorities: Opposes Trump’s tariffs and the war in Iran. Supports an all-of-the-above approach to energy production, including green energy, natural gas and nuclear.
Resume: First elected to Congress in 2016. Retired to run for governor in 2022, lost the primary to Gov. Kathy Hochul. Re-elected to his old seat in 2024 after Congress expelled Rep. George Santos.
Quote: “I will fight for you against the extremists.”
Mike LiPetri, Republican
Policy priorities: Supports deporting undocumented immigrants with criminal records. Opposes boycotts of Israel and regulations on cryptocurrency.
Resume: Served in the state Assembly from 2019-2021. Ran for this seat in 2024 and lost to Suozzi.
Quote: “I stood up to the radical left agenda that threatened our quality of life and drove up our cost of living.”
4th District, Nassau County
Laura Gillen, Democrat (incumbent)
Policy priorities: Supports eliminating the cap on the state and local tax deduction, and extending temporary protected status for Haitians living in the United States. Opposes cuts to Medicaid.
Resume: First elected to the seat in 2024. Former town supervisor of Hempstead.
Quote: “My number one priority is representing Long Islanders, not Trump.”
Jeanine Driscoll, Republican
Policy priorities: Supports restoring the full state and local tax deduction and strengthening the United States' border with Mexico.
Resume: Town of Hempstead receiver of taxes, first elected in 2019.
Quote: “There’s a lot of middle-class people in the district who need relief that’s not being offered to them right now through the current representation.”
1st District, Suffolk County
Nick LaLota, Republican (incumbent)
Policy priorities: Supports deporting undocumented immigrants with criminal records and tax cuts. Opposes offshore drilling on Long Island.
Resume: First elected to Congress in 2022. Served three deployments overseas as a naval officer.
Quote: “My mission is simple: to make Suffolk safer and more affordable for every family that calls this amazing place home.”
Christopher Gallant, Democrat
Policy priorities: Supports developing more housing near transit stations, refinancing federal student loans, and expanding child tax credits.
Resume: Former Army pilot and air traffic controller local union president.
Quote: “I’m not running to make noise. I’m running to do the work.”
11th District, Staten Island and South Brooklyn
Nicole Malliotakis, Republican (incumbent)
Policy priorities: Increase funding for the Department of Homeland Security and ICE. Suspend the federal gas tax to reduce energy costs.
Resume: First elected to the House in 2020. Previously served in the state Assembly.
Quote: “I said I was going to fight to secure our border and deport criminals from our streets and that’s exactly what we did.”
Mike DeCillis, Democrat
Policy priorities: Raise the corporate tax rate and create a single-payer healthcare system.
Resume: Former first responder, NYPD officer and special education teacher.
Quote: “I know that everyone in the district deserves to have their voice heard in government, and that they are currently not.”
results.summary:
New York voters head to the polls on November 3 to decide key races for governor, attorney general, and several competitive congressional seats across the state.

### Key Points
- Election Day is November 3, with polls open from 6 a.m. to 9 p.m., following an early voting period from October 24 to November 1.
- Gubernatorial candidates include incumbent Democrat Kathy Hochul and Republican challenger Bruce Blakeman, while Attorney General Letitia James faces Republican Saritha Komatireddy.
- State Comptroller Tom DiNapoli is seeking re-election against Republican challenger Joseph Hernandez.
- New York City voters will decide on five ballot questions regarding city contracting, road safety, building permits, and fiscal resilience.
- Competitive congressional races include the 1st, 3rd, 4th, 11th, and 17th districts, featuring candidates like Mike Lawler, Tom Suozzi, and Laura Gillen.

### Why it Matters
These elections will determine the leadership and policy direction of New York State, impacting everything from housing and tax policy to public safety and immigration enforcement. The results of these contests, particularly in key congressional districts, could also influence the balance of power in the U.S. House of Representatives.

results.title: Goldman Sachs sees AI-fueled layoffs displacing nearly 10% of workers
results.author: jsor@businessinsider.com (Jennifer Sor)
results.content:
The outlook for AI's impact on the job market is dim, but Goldman Sachs put a number on just how many people could be impacted by the technology.
Economists at Goldman updated their forecast for how many jobs could be impacted as companies turn to artificial intelligence to power their workforce. In Goldman's baseline scenario, which has productivity rising 15% in the US and other developed economies, the bank sees up to 9% of workers being displaced from their current roles.
Last year, Goldmans' chief economist Jan Hatzius said AI could displace 6% to 7% of all US workers. The bank began to float a displacement rate as high as 9% as this summer, which would be equivalent to around 15 million workers who see their jobs disrupted by AI.
The job market may also face headwinds from slower hiring overall because of AI adoption, though the hit to overall unemployment will likely be fueled more by outright job losses rather than less hiring, the report added.
"Under our baseline forecasts for near potential growth next year, our estimates suggest that AI labor disruption will likely only gradually increase rather than delivering an abrupt labor market shock," Hatzius wrote in a report on Thursday.
The US is still in the early stages of AI adoption. Less than a quarter of firms have incorporated AI into regular workflows, Goldman estimates.
Hatzius said AI adoption may speed up if the US economy were to enter an economic downturn, citing its analysis of past automation cycles during recessions.
"A more concerning takeaway from our analysis is that a cyclical slowdown would likely accelerate AI-related automation and job losses, thereby amplifying the broader business cycle," he wrote.
The panic about AI job losses has eased slightly, but the idea that AI could one day decimate entry-level white-collar work is still a fear voiced by some researchers.
Layoff announcements ticked lower in September, but AI remains the top cited reason for job cuts, accounting for 21% of all announced layoffs. Job losses in the tech sector also outpace that of any other industry, accounting for 29% of all job cuts last month, according to the data from Challenger, Gray & Christmas.
results.summary:
Goldman Sachs economists estimate that artificial intelligence could displace up to 9% of workers in developed economies, potentially impacting approximately 15 million jobs as automation technology adoption increases.

### Key Points
- Goldman Sachs projects that AI-driven productivity gains could lead to the displacement of 9% of the workforce in the United States and other developed nations.
- The bank’s chief economist, Jan Hatzius, noted that this disruption will likely occur gradually rather than through an abrupt labor market shock.
- Currently, less than 25% of firms have integrated artificial intelligence into their regular business workflows.
- Data from Challenger, Gray & Christmas indicates that AI was cited as the primary reason for 21% of all announced job cuts in September.
- The technology sector currently leads all industries in job losses, accounting for 29% of total layoffs reported last month.

### Why it Matters
This forecast highlights the growing tension between corporate productivity gains and long-term workforce stability as businesses increasingly prioritize automation. If economic conditions worsen, the acceleration of AI adoption could amplify job losses and significantly alter the landscape for entry-level white-collar roles.

results.title: Capcom and Square Enix Suffer Online Attacks As Hackers Access Player Data
results.author: Alicia Haddick
results.content:
A number of services run by Capcom and Square Enix have been the subject of unauthorized access attacks by third-party individuals and groups, part of a surge of AI-powered cybersecurity breaches of Japanese companies in recent weeks.
On October 19, Square Enix confirmed that a number of Final Fantasy XIV accounts had been accessed by an unnamed third party. According to the developer, access to the accounts was not the result of a direct breach of Square Enix’s own security and databases, but a result of this third party using credentials gathered from the security breaches of other companies to access these accounts. The company has already stepped in to prevent access to accounts it thinks may be compromised, but has warned that it may enforce password resets and security measures on all accounts if such breaches continue to increase.
Meanwhile, Capcom disclosed yesterday that a direct breach of databases and services containing user information had occurred, resulting in access to system-identifying account information and email addresses for over 11.7 million users. More notably, in at least 43 cases, access to user information including date of birth, gender, and location have been breached, and in roughly 196 accounts, passwords were illegally changed. This breach occurred on October 19th, with the vulnerability immediately fixed internally. An investigation was conducted to learn the cause of this breach, with all information being handed to police.
Notably, these two incidents are not the only cases of cybersecurity breaches targeting Japanese companies in recent weeks. The Japanese government is looking into methods to address the growing number of breaches for companies in all sectors, with cases of such breaches in 2026 already surpassing the total for all of last year. Many of these breaches have been powered by AI systems.
The regularity of these breaches is a reminder to ensure that your passwords are not repeated across services and that you update all passwords at regular intervals. If the service supports it, two-factor authentication should also be applied to make your personal data more secure, and to ensure that any data acquired in the breach of one company can’t then be used to break into your accounts elsewhere.
results.summary:
Capcom and Square Enix have reported significant cybersecurity breaches involving unauthorized account access and data theft, highlighting a growing trend of AI-powered attacks targeting major Japanese corporations.

### Key Points
- Capcom confirmed a database breach on October 19 exposing email addresses and system-identifying information for over 11.7 million users.
- The Capcom incident resulted in 196 accounts having passwords illegally changed and 43 users suffering the theft of personal details like birth dates and locations.
- Square Enix reported unauthorized access to Final Fantasy XIV accounts caused by credential stuffing, where attackers used login data stolen from other companies.
- Japanese government officials report that cybersecurity breaches in 2026 have already surpassed the total number of incidents recorded throughout the entirety of 2025.

### Why it Matters
These incidents underscore the critical vulnerability of cross-platform credential reuse in an era where AI-driven attacks are rapidly increasing in frequency and sophistication. Users are encouraged to adopt unique passwords and two-factor authentication to protect their personal data from being compromised across multiple services.

results.title: The Rise and Fall of Jev
results.author: Alex Ewerlöf
results.content:
This is a quick note on how the industry’s reaction to Jev reveals the desperate state of AI. I’ll dissect:
- What is Jev, how was it hyped and why it spread like mass hysteria? Jev isn’t dead but its hype cycle is. Decision models are on the rise.
- What are the noteworthy innovations since ChatGPT brought “AI” to the mainstream?
- Why is the industry starved from real innovation and what high impact problems are still unsolved after 4 years of revolution incremental improvements?
The point is to use Jev’s hype cycle to call out the manipulative marketing that are too familiar with at this point.
Jev
You probably don’t need an intro to Jev at this time because since its introduction 33 days ago, it has been all the rage!
But if you were clever enough to ignore it, here’s what actually matters:
Jev is basically a general purpose classifier (e.g. quick judgement). What makes it interesting is that you don’t have to train it with a lot of data (although that lack of special-purpose training negatively impacts its utility).
Calling it a “decision model” is a bit far fetched especially since it cannot even see (rival open-weight models have multi-modal features) or reason (that’s how it’s so cheap).
The idea behind Jev isn’t new! The idea of non-autoregressive decision models with RL goes back more than a year ago. The original author is pissed but as we’ll see drama is an inseparable part of AI hype.
Hype
I want to walk you through the emotional roller-coaster I went through when I read their announcement via hackernews:
At OpenAI, I helped build the methods that made language models useful at following instructions and talking with people. That work ended up as the research behind ChatGPT.
😎 So the founder was behind ChatGPT, one of the fastest-growing products in history. I’m listening…
At the time, I thought maybe chat models would lead to AGI, but despite the hype it became obvious to me that there was something really big missing.
😃 Oh, my god! This is it! ChatGPT is missing something big and he’s about to reveal it! We’re one step closer to AGI if we haven’t reached it already! I’m thrilled to read more…
After two years in stealth, countless technical challenges, and research breakthroughs… I am beyond excited to announce
😱 Spit it out! I’m beyond excited to read this…
TypeSafe AI is releasing our first System One Model
😯 Wait what?!! “System one”?
Do you understand what you’re talking about? Here’s my recollection of how Daniel Kahneman defined the two systems:
- System one: fast, cheap (in terms of computational power), emotional, unconscious and judgmental.
- System two: slow, expensive (takes more brain power), logical, conscious, and more elaborate.
If Jev is system one then LM is system two? It can’t even handle logical reasoning!
Most importantly Jev came with another interesting framing:
can’t hallucinate
Hallucination is one of the biggest problems with the current generation of language models but no hallucination doesn’t mean the response is logically correct. In Jev’s context, it just means that the output matches the schema.
Technically conventional language models can gain this ability by bolting a control loop (e.g., type checker, JSON schema parser) on top. Jev does this much faster and without reasoning. It’s in the name:
We named Jev after William Stanley Jevons. We expect machine intelligence to follow a similar path to coal, after steam-engine efficiency led to an increase in demand.
I don’t know Jev’s architecture because in the true ex-"Open”AI employee tradition, not much is released (probably in the name of “safety” or “moat”). But that doesn’t stop them from dropping jargons:
We built a new […] training method we call Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD).
Note: RLCD rhymes with the “traditional” methods:
- RLHF: Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback
- RLVR: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
They even claim:
Jev is neither small nor an LLM, hence being off the intelligence Pareto curve.
Fortunately, there’s no shortage of similar models, some of them with even better performance (Laya, Kev, Nimble, NanoJev, etc.)
So let me sum up the marketing strategy:
- Name dropping: former ChatGPT creator, Jevons’ paradox, Pareto curve, System one
- Big claim: cannot hallucinate, exponentially faster and cheaper, entirely new stack, amazing benchmarks and demos
- Ambiguity and jargon: no useful implementation details on the “new training algorithm” or RLCD dataset
- Drama: Laya showed this idea in 1.5 years prior to Jev’s launch
OK, I think at this point we’ve seen this pattern enough to recognize it. I actually think Jev’s team kicked it up a notch to a comical level. Whether their marketing is written by LLM or not, they nailed it.
Fortunately, Jev’s initial noise died off almost at the same speed that it blew up. I can only speculate that as more people experimented with it, we realized:
- It cannot hallucinate, but it can still be wrong. It is even more wrong than conventional language models, and in that sense “system one” is the right naming. Although I consider all current generations of language models system one (even the reasoning models) because they do not really reason in the sense that’s expected of system two.
- It is cheaper, but there are open-weight models that beat it in performance/cost ratio (depending on the task). What makes Jev different than frontier-level LLMs is the fact that you can actually run it at the edge (e.g. locally) with matching quality.
Jev is not completely hype, we just went from “Peak of Inflated Expectations” to the “Trough of Disillusionment” in record time:
It’s not dead. Some companies use it while I believe the majority of use cases are addressed by open-weight rivals.
I really don’t want to bash Jev. Instead I want to use it as an example of where we are, as an industry.
Incremental improvements
I was one of the lucky few who got access to GPT-2 when it was invitation-only.
As a senior tech lead, I allocate part of my time to scout new tech and experiment in order to stay relevant. Prior to that, I had experienced IBM Watson and a bunch of other products so it wasn’t a big deal for me personally.
I was actually underwhelmed by GPT-2 because at the time it could:
- Summarize text
- Predict what comes after a piece of text
- … that was it really! 😄 I don’t remember more than that. So I moved on…
Then I saw someone create a turn-based dialogue from one of these models and to spice it up, they added an avatar to it. I thought it was creepy and funny.
Then Blake Lemoine came out claiming Google’s language model named LaMDA was conscious. Unsurprisingly, this started a philosophical discussion that’s still ongoing on the side. Again, I didn’t give it too much thought.
BUT, Sam Altman, having spent a few years at the startup accelerator (Y Combinator), saw an opportunity. Specifically the chat application seems to have got his attention and soon ChatGPT was announced.
At the time, I thought it was a cool way to turn their token prediction model into a user-friendly product for the masses.
Personally, I couldn’t use it seriously because:
- Poor quality: it didn’t know what it didn’t know, so it just winged it (AKA hallucination). Although the rise of “prompt engineering” and “reasoning models” promised to reduce this issue.
- Privacy: I had been working with computers for 2+ decades at the time and live by the mantra that “if it’s possible, assume it happened”. Meaning if OpenAI is technically capable of storing my conversation, I cannot trust it enough to share any company IP or private information with it.
I vividly remember the backlash Google got for their multi-modal demo when people realized it wasn’t recorded in real-time! Those were the days when even a small deception would be a conspiracy.
When llama.cpp came out I got a gaming machine with an NVIDIA card (AI machines weren’t a thing back then) to build with AI.
Meanwhile people discovered that language models can generate code It was tedious to copy/paste it so we got the early versions of a harness.
Quickly after, we got “function calls” which allowed the models to do stuff!
I was using VS Code at the time and the hype was hard to ignore even though my company at the time had a strict policy against using AI tools (yes! hard to believe that just 3-4 years ago companies prioritized IP over velocity).
I remember paying for a Copilot subscription out of pocket and using VS Code insider on my open source projects.
I was so frustrated that I shared this meme on the company Slack:
Meanwhile there was drama at OpenAI (Ilya was part of a coup that fired their CEO, then Satya was playing 4D chess while Elon was lawyering up). It was a sh*tshow which is exactly how it managed to capture the interest of non-techies, a trend that continues to today with “almighty rogue AI” hacking others while whistle-blowers and alarmists rise speak of existential threat!
Simultaneously premature AI products were creating dramas of their own (assisting crimes, cheating, etc.) and AI bros anthropomorphize the tool as if it had desires of its own (my read: they want to judge accountability).
There’s also circular investment, pentagon drama, chip wars, autonomous killer drones, etc. but in the spirit of brevity, let’s stick to the technical side of things.
Then Peter Steinberger, a veteran developer who was away from computers due to burnout, created an AI companion, which brought the Agents (LM that can do stuff) to the mainstream.
So far I’ve covered:
- Instruction-tuned models
- Function calls
- Coding harnesses
- AI agents
Let’s speed through the other incremental improvements:
- Larger parameter size unlocks emergent properties that are hard to explain by analyzing the micro level architecture (mostly leading to sophisticated perceived behavior but also jagged alignment).
- Larger context windows improve accuracy (although the practical limit is much smaller than the theoretical size).
- Multimodal models enable generating voice, music, pictures, and videos while increasingly more models can understand these modalities.
- MCP abstracts away the implementation and enables different AI products to use the tools needed to do productive work.
- ACP, sub-agents and various orchestration techniques allow larger tasks to be planned and broken into smaller pieces.
- Sandboxes help improve security and isolate unwanted side effects of agentic workflows and when they fall short, there’s HITL (but we still haven’t solved the approval fatigue).
- Skills, web search and web access allow agents to access information that’s outside their training data or knowledge cut-off date.
- Various memory architectures and consolidation techniques enable the models to recall what they learn.
- Chinese labs showed us more efficient ways to train and run the models.
- Feedback loops and scratchpads improve the model’s perceived quality by running part of the verification closer to the model.
This is good progress, no question about it. But I think a part of the reason AI is a hot topic is all the drama surrounding it:
- Geopolitics: unlike the US economy which is primarily service-based, China is a manufacturing behemoth. Up until DeepSeek discovered that it can manipulate stock and AI investment by diffusing the compute equation, I don’t think China had a solid AI plan. Now they do. Good old American sanctions target their chip import but China (being run by engineers) made huge strides recently both in chip manufacturing but also in model architecture. Meanwhile AI is used in warfare from drones to intelligence (and mass surveillance back home). In the best seller How the mighty falls, Collins lists 5 stages of demise: a) Hubris Born of Success, b) Undisciplined Pursuit of More, c) Denial of Risk and Peril, d) Grasping for Salvation, e) Capitulation to Irrelevance or Death. Those same stages apply to a falling empires and in this case US has bet big on AI while China diffuses US’s massive bet with open-weight models. Consumers win for now.
- Debt bubble: You can read more on Bloomberg but it basically boils down to a series of interdependent bets that is so large it impacts the national GDP. It has to work regardless of how much IP has to be stolen and how many lies have to be told. The stakes are too high at this point.
- Safety: we got used to the “rogue AI” narrative where the AI vendors aren’t held accountable for breaking into other companies and government institutes. Why would we? It’s an open secret that the training data wasn’t legally obtained anyway (and there are multiple class action lawsuits to prove that). On top of it, there have been multiple cases where people lost their lives due to AI — and I’m not even counting “vibe war”. (yes, I actually put an em-dash there!) 🙃
- Impact on jobs: software engineering is low-hanging fruit for AI automation due to its nature (there’s plenty of training data, and the tools are often on a language model’s home turf). There have been discussions of UBI (universal basic income) and UHI (universal high income) but looking at the benevolence of the billionaires running the show, I don’t buy it at all.
AI is hot, because it can potentially impact all of us. But we have to remember one simple fact:
Humans are fundamentally flawed when it comes to predicting the future.
Most notoriously, we have difficulty understanding the S-curve (meaning the pace of change is slow at the beginning and end).
And with prominent scientists leaving their lucrative positions to slow down the pace of development, we really cannot be sure about how long it will take for AI to really manifest the changes, if ever.
What’s missing?
With all the incremental improvements of the past few years, we still haven’t solved some fundamental problems.
Here’s a short list of what I consider truly game changing:
- Abstract reasoning: neural networks (not just language models) are prone to making stuff up (hallucination). The state of the industry has improved a lot since hands had 5+ fingers and videos were easy to detect, but the closest we’ve come to a true system 2 is to pair the models with code and still the feedback loops and human intervention are necessary.
- Continuous learning: auxiliary context (e.g. skills, grounding, search and various model architectures) has come a long way but we’re far from the state where the models learn in real time. By extension, the next generation of AI should learn from fewer samples, data and repetitions.
- Embodiment: while there have been great improvements in robotic body form factor, we’re still not at a point where AI is rapid and efficient enough to be put in a robot body and react to the sensory stimuli in real time or expose fine motoric control and navigate the 3D world with enough prevision to take over “simple” human chores.
- Economics of running AI: Jensen Huang talks about installing “Gigawatts” of compute as if it’s normal to measure temperature in kilometers/hour!!! The truth is: our brain delivers AGI level intelligence at 20 Watts and until we solve that problem, there is not enough water, power and data centers that can realistically make massive change in workforce. Unfortunately, we live in a post-truth world where hysteria, personalized propaganda and mass psychosis have an oversized impact on the dominant discourse so we’re all supposed to be scared and distracted. The economics makes even less sense if we expect embodied AI (robots) to replace even a fraction of human population. Unlike bots, our organic bodies return to nature and participate in the nature’s recycling system much faster than metals and plastic that build a robot. Sometimes I feel we forgot that we’re living on a tiny rock with finite resources which get increasingly harder to extract.
All of this, is not to say that AI won’t be used to:
- Robosoldiers and robocops
- Generate new diseases
- Connect mass surveillance to personalized propaganda
- Corporate espionage and mass penetration into computer systems
- etc.
The truth is: you don’t need AGI-level of intelligence to cause destruction. The current generation of AI, paired with harness, tools and skills is plenty capable of causing damage in the wrong hands.
And if you think this is not happening already, I know a guy who gives free ice cream in his basement! 🙃
Recap
I think Jev is a good example of how great marketing fizzed out in the face of reality.
- Is it useful? Yes.
- Is it relevant? Yes.
- Is it dead? Just its hype.
- Is it revolutionary? Depends on your cost, quality, speed triangle.
- Is it as big as it was claimed? I hope you have the answer by now.
If I had a magic wand, I would want us all to step back and see the holistic arc of recent events and calm down a little. The red flags are easy to see:
- Name dropping: builds a bridge between the new unknown to the trusted known.
- Jargon: makes you feel stupid for not having the context.
- Ambiguity: lets your brain fill in the blanks and if you’re an optimist, you’re at risk of getting overly excited and eventually disappointed
- Inflate expectations: big claims require big evidence. Don’t trust the isolated benchmarks that do not resemble how YOU would actually use it, especially if the benchmark is coming from the same entity that has a conflict of interest.
- Drama: engages human emotion to what would otherwise be a logical technical decision. “All publicity is good publicity”.
Unfortunately, I think that ship might have already sailed and in the age of mass-produced synthetic content and personalized propaganda, maybe we’re too stressed to think straight.
Maybe LLMs are “system two”, after all, if we collectively lose our critical thinking and let our emotions be manipulated with the kind of marketing and manipulation we’ve seen too much lately.
Someone shared this on Hackernews (thank you 🙌) and it went all the way up to 2nd spot.
The early comments came at agentic speed and were unanimously focused on two things: 1) anecdotes about Jev being alive, and conveniently ignoring competition, 2) taking it personal and making it personal as if killing the messenger will make the message false. Weird. 🤔
My monetization strategy is to give away most content for free but these posts take anywhere from a few hours to a few days to draft, edit, research, illustrate, and publish. I pull these hours from my private time, vacation days and weekends. The simplest way to support this work is to like, subscribe and share it. If you really want to support me in lifting our community, you can consider a paid subscription. If you want to save, you can get 20% off via this link. As a token of appreciation, subscribers get full access to the Pro-Tips sections and my online book Reliability Engineering Mindset. Your contribution also funds my open-source products like Service Level Calculator. You can also invite your friends to gain free access or save via a group subscription.
And to those of you who already support me, thank you for sponsoring this content for the others. 🙌 If you have questions or feedback, or you want me to dig deeper into something, please let me know in the comments.

The rapid rise and fall of the Jev AI model highlights a broader industry trend of using aggressive marketing and technical jargon to inflate expectations for incremental innovations.

### Key Points
- Jev is a general-purpose classifier marketed as a "System One" decision model, though it lacks the reasoning capabilities of advanced language models.
- The product launch relied on high-profile associations with ChatGPT creators and complex terminology like "Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions" (RLCD).
- Despite claims of being a revolutionary breakthrough, Jev faces stiff competition from existing open-weight models that offer superior performance-to-cost ratios.
- The hype cycle surrounding Jev mirrors a recurring pattern in the AI sector where dramatic announcements often mask a lack of significant technical differentiation.
- Fundamental challenges in AI, such as true abstract reasoning, continuous real-time learning, and energy-efficient embodiment, remain largely unsolved.

### Why it Matters
The Jev hype cycle serves as a case study for how manipulative marketing and industry drama can distract from the reality of slow, incremental progress in artificial intelligence. Investors and users must look past the jargon to distinguish between genuine technological breakthroughs and products designed to capitalize on current market hysteria.

results.title: China targets 2030 for its national blockchain network buildout
results.author: Cointelegraph by Yohan Yun
results.content:
China targets 2030 for its national blockchain network buildout
China’s five-year digital development plan calls for wider blockchain use in trade and manufacturing alongside stronger technical standards.
China has set a 2030 target for largely completing a national blockchain network under a five-year digital development plan published Friday.
The 15th Five-Year Plan for National Informatization, which sets priorities calls for deeper blockchain use in trade and finance in the Yangtze River Delta, and deployment at scale in manufacturing and agriculture in the Chengdu–Chongqing region in southwestern China.
Friday’s plan was issued by the Central Cyberspace Affairs Commission, a senior body within the ruling Communist Party that coordinates digital development policy.
The document makes the completion target explicit for a project already included in China’s national development plan released in March. A joint policy from the Communist Party’s central leadership and State Council published on Oct. 9 called for its construction.
The new plan also calls for stronger blockchain technical standards and greater use of the technology in data circulation and trading.
Mainland China bans cryptocurrency-related business activities, but promotes blockchain technology as a national priority.
In October 2019, President Xi Jinping called for greater investment in blockchain and identified it as an important area for developing China’s own technological capabilities.

results.title: Why Meta is charging to post more hyperlinks
results.author: Cooper Katz McKim
results.content:
Why Meta is charging to post more hyperlinks
You're reading a newsletter from The Indicator from Planet Money. Once a week, we curate our favorite stories and insights on business, finance, economics and why they matter. Subscribe here to get it in your inbox every Friday.
Outside of Atlanta, two gas stations got into a price war. The Atlanta TV station WSB-TV reported that, over the course of a day, prices dropped from $2.54 down to $1.44, $1.39 and eventually down to just 97 cents. When drivers took notice, the traffic jam began and police intervened. BUT while it was happening, one driver said she only spent $15 to fill up her truck. It usually costs $90. "Look at God, baby! Look at God!" she said.
In our team's Slack, co-host Wailin Wong responded to the low prices, "make it up on volume!?" Jeff Guo wrote, "how is this real." But like, actually. How is this real?
Coming up:
- Why Facebook is charging you to post hyperlinks
- How fake data centers can still drive up electricity costs
- How one man is dealing with a rental car agency
News We're Watching
Why websites make it hard to leave
What To Know: Social media sites don't love it when users leave. If you've ever used Instagram, it's not the easiest place to post links. You need to include them in bios, or through a special button on stories. Well now, if you run a Facebook page, you can only post TWO hyperlinks for free per month. $49.99/month will get you a Meta One Advanced plan, allowing you to include eight hyperlinks in posts or reels. With the $499/month Max plan, you can post an unlimited amount. Ashley Gullen, who runs a game design company, posted on Mastodon, a decentralized social media platform, "Facebook achieving absurd new heights of enshittification" in response to the news. This isn't totally unique. Nieman Lab did a whole study finding that posting links hurts news publishers on X.
Why are companies doing this?: Attention is money for social media sites. They want to keep you inside their walls! David Evans, managing director at BRG, a consulting firm, wrote a simple explanation as to why platforms want you to stay on their site: "Attention platforms use content to get consumers to spend time on their platform and sell marketers the ability to expose these consumers to messages."
Even FAKE data centers could be driving up electricity costs - The Wall Street Journal
What To Know: Developers are desperate to get their data centers up and running. They need it to help power their precious AI and whatever other computing is needed. BUT, developers won't just say, "This is the only location we'll accept for this project." No, they'll put out requests to all sorts of locations for their centers. The problem is, utilities are still considering data centers that likely WON'T GET BUILT in their electricity forecasts. Energy research firm Wood Mackenzie estimates that only a mere 23% of data-center requests are considered "high confidence," according to The Wall Street Journal. The rest are speculative!
How this affects YOU: Electricity costs could rise even if the data centers don't get built. Hoowwwwww does that work now? Because utilities are still planning for expected demand. They can't just suddenly integrate a wildly power-demanding data center without new substations or transmission lines. It's possible for the utility to pass on some of those grid investments onto consumers, even if the data centers never come to pass. Some power markets also set prices based on future demand so… There are lots of ways these projects could mess with your electricity bill.
Another oil reserve gets tapped - U.S. Department of Energy
It's your weekly update on diesel prices! This week, the Trump administration has found a NEW way to try and lower prices, which seems to be a core issue ahead of the midterms. This time, the U.S. Department of Energy has authorized an exchange from the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve. It would release roughly a third of the reserves for heating oil. The Chief Energy Advisor for Gulf Oil thinks it won't make a difference on prices.
What's interesting, this reserve has only been tapped ONCE, and that was after Hurricane Sandy. According to the DOE's history, that's the sort of thing it was meant for. "The intent was to create a buffer large enough to allow commercial companies to compensate for interruptions in supply during severe winter weather." Here, the DOE will loan out up to 315,000 barrels of heating oil in hopes of lowering prices. It's called an exchange because borrowing entities, like a regional heating oil retailer, would be required to replace the same volume at a premium ahead of next year.
Today's Indicator
Why Oracle's debt load could be your problem
If you HAVEN'T listened: We keep hearing about the AI boom that's propping up the U.S. economy. Well, Oracle is a part of that story. The enterprise software company has moved into building out data centers to serve the AI industry. Now, they have a huge deal with OpenAI worth $300 billion over five years. Here's the problem. Oracle has been spending freely with the assumption that this OpenAI deal will deliver. But what if it doesn't? Oracle already has $169 billion in total debt and a growing credit risk. They're one link in an interconnected chain of enormous tech companies. If that link breaks, it could spell trouble for the economy.
If you HAVE listened: Lindsay Tyler, credit analyst, explains in the piece that Oracle is making a bet on data centers. "The analogy might be you have 10 apartments, you've pre-signed leases with, for those 10 apartments, and you're thinking, 'Should I build another floor?'"
On the surface, this doesn't seem plausible. Isn't computing demand insatiable right now? Yeah, right now. But…
- AI is getting so much more efficient to run. Research from Epoch AI found "the cost of achieving a given level of AI performance has fallen about 47% per quarter since 2023, or 13× per year."
- The chips powering these AI models "have a useful lifespan of one to three years due to rapid technological obsolescence and physical wear."
Some economic historians like to compare the AI buildout to the railroads, but this one is different. Rails last longer than one to three years. The cost of shipping does not plummet 13x per year. And maybe Oracle is at the center of these economic forces colliding: a railroad-type investment boom building castles made of sand.
Rest of the Week
We can inflate away the national debt… at a cost
Listener Mailbag
Context: Last week, we ran an episode full of consumer rage stories. One included a story about someone charged for damage to a rental car that was impossible to disprove. Stay to the end for a surprising twist.
Listener Jim Zerefos sent in a response from Colorado.
I share the frustration of the person who complained about dubious damage claims from a rental car company. I've been fighting Alamo for nearly a year now over a $1,600 damage claim. Alamo sent me photos of very minor damage taken AFTER our rental, but never provided photos from BEFORE our rental. [The car] had some 23k miles so seems possible (likely?) the scratches occurred some time before our rental.
My spidey sense here smells a scam: "rental companies now scan cars for damage and so are trying to find scapegoats for all prior damage"? Alamo's reaction to me (and my insurance company) has been to ignore us - never sending the "before" pics and never acknowledging that's an issue. They just keep sending us invoices. They now are threatening collection action and have banned me from renting from the Alamo rental family (as if I would). So, the story on the broader scam? Or story on which credit cards still offer primary rental damage coverage (which we THOUGHT we had)?
By the way, here at The Indicator, we reached out to the car rental company and they responded in a statement through a spokesperson from Enterprise Mobility: "Customer satisfaction is our top priority, and we are always open to further conversations with customers regarding damage claims. Our team is actively reviewing this matter through our escalation process and will reach out to the customer to share an update today."
And we already have an update: Jim tells us Alamo has since dropped the claim and will make no further collection efforts. Alamo's "risk" department instructed the Cleveland manager to drop the claim, according to Jim.
Jim's response: "Sad to see that you got more action in a day than my insurance company and I got in nearly a year."
In Our Spare Time
Co-host Wailin Wong is reading Under Story
This fall has yielded a bumper crop of big new fiction releases. My favorite from the last couple of weeks of reading is UNDER STORY by Chloe Benjamin. This novel is about a fungi expert who goes to Antarctica after a family tragedy. She's hoping to anonymously wash dishes at a research station. However, a strange light phenomenon and the arrival of her physicist ex-husband pull her back into the scientific world. This was an exciting, imaginative, and beautiful story about grief, family, parallel universes, trees, and mushrooms. (Bonus rec: This book also makes for a good pairing with Emily St. John Mandel's new novel, Exit Party.)

What you need to know
- Oura and Ultrahuman find themselves in another dispute as the former sues over "patent infringements."
- Oura states Ultrahuman infringed on "design and internal component" patents with the Ring Pro.
- In 2025, Ultrahuman sued Oura for "ripping off" its patented health tech.
Oura is reportedly suing Ultrahuman over its Ring Pro. The company alleges Ultrahuman infringed a few patents when it created the device.
A report by TechCrunch highlighted the lawsuit between Oura and Ultrahuman. The latter claims Ultrahuman infringed on its "design and internal component" patents with the Ring Pro. In a statement to the publication, an Oura spokesperson said, "Ultrahuman has a history of copying Oura’s innovations, as demonstrated by the 2025 ITC ruling against the company." It adds, "Ultrahuman introduced a redesigned ring but failed to address continued infringement of Oura’s patents."
Specifically, Oura says it's suing Ultrahuman over the ring's "curved battery, circuit board, magnets, and sensors." However, as the publication notes, Oura was granted this internal-component patent (12,769,363) on October 20. The lawsuit was filed two days later.
Ultrahuman has struggled to get its products to U.S. consumers. The post reminds us of an import ban it faced, which forced its presence out of the country. The Ultrahuman Ring Pro was its ticket back into the market; however, Oura wants to stop that from happening. What's more, the company is reportedly seeking "monetary damages" in this lawsuit.
Ultrahuman's co-founder and CEO, Mohit Kumar, told TechCrunch, "Oura has now chosen to assert different patents, including one that was issued just two days before this lawsuit was filed." Presently, Kumar says courts have not stopped it from selling the Ring Pro to U.S. consumers, so it remains available even today.
Back & Forth
These two companies have gone back and forth for years now. In 2025, Ultrahuman sued Oura. It accused Oura's Ring 4 of "ripping off its patented smart ring tech." The core of this dispute concerned "sleep tracking, circadian tools, and women’s health features." Ultrahuman said it "pioneered" those features. There was also a major difference between the two companies.
While Ultrahuman offers its features without a paywall through PowerPlugs, Oura features a subscription-heavy model. Ultrahuman also clarified why it was suing Oura. It said that defending its patents wasn't the primary goal. Instead, "positioning itself as a defender of open health data and Indian innovation on the global stage" was more important to the company.
Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android
Ultrahuman has continued to do just that in 2026. The company partnered with HealthEx, which brings users' official medical records into the app. You can compare your smart ring's data against your medical records and take those insights to your doctor. Earlier in October, it rolled out Heart Scan for the Ring Pro. Heart Scan needs sixty seconds to deliver a snapshot of your heart's condition at a moment's notice.
Nickolas is always excited about tech and getting his hands on it. Writing for him can vary from delivering the latest tech story to scribbling in his journal. When Nickolas isn't hitting a story, he's often grinding away at a game or chilling with a book in his hand.
