Oura has filed a patent infringement lawsuit against competitor Ultrahuman, alleging that the Ring Pro device utilizes proprietary designs and internal components protected by Oura’s recent intellectual property.

### Key Points
- Oura filed the lawsuit on October 22, 2025, just two days after receiving patent 12,769,363 for internal ring components.
- The legal complaint targets specific Ring Pro hardware, including the curved battery, circuit board, magnets, and integrated sensors.
- Ultrahuman CEO Mohit Kumar stated that the Ring Pro remains available for purchase in the United States despite the ongoing litigation.
- This legal action follows a 2025 dispute where Ultrahuman accused Oura of copying its own health-tracking technology and features.
- Oura is seeking monetary damages, citing a history of alleged patent infringement by Ultrahuman regarding smart ring innovations.

### Why it Matters
This ongoing legal battle highlights the intensifying competition and high stakes within the rapidly growing smart ring market. As companies fight to protect their intellectual property, these lawsuits could influence product availability and the pace of innovation for wearable health technology.

results.title: Beyond the Review: Inside the Onyx RCR 80V E-Bike
results.author: Joseph Kaminski
results.content:
The first thing people ask about the Onyx RCR 80V is how fast it goes. After hundreds of miles around New York, I’m more interested in what this electric bike is like to live with.
The acceleration certainly gets your attention. But so do the compact proportions, CarPlay, cruise control and little design decisions that become more noticeable the longer you ride. Then there are the bigger questions: Can you repair it? Will parts still be available? What happens when the technology gets old?
My impression is that Onyx is trying to build a compact electric motorbike with BMX-inspired maneuverability and modern electronics, while leaving owners room to customize it and keep it running. Riding the RCR and talking with Onyx founder Tim Seward helped me understand that approach. Whether it holds up over years of ownership is a question a few hundred miles can’t answer.
More from CNET
Onyx RCR 80V GeekBox
Manufacturer figures below are advertised specifications, not independently measured performance results. Prices as of Oct. 14.
| Specification | Onyx RCR 80V | 
| Starting price | $4,699 Street / $4,899 Dual Sport | 
| Motor | Rear hub; advertised 8kW nominal | 
| Battery | Removable 80V, 45Ah / 3.6kWh | 
| Claimed top speed | 65–75 mph, depending on configuration; advertised for off-road use | 
| Claimed maximum range | 140 miles; current table associates this with Cruise Tune Eco at 15 mph | 
| Claimed acceleration | 0–30 mph in 1.7 seconds | 
| Ride modes tested | Eco, Normal, Sport and Hyper | 
| Wheels | 17-inch tubeless | 
| Brakes | Hydraulic discs with 220mm rotors | 
| Display | TFT touchscreen | 
| Phone integration | Apple CarPlay / Android Auto | 
| Other features | Reverse, cruise control, regenerative braking, turn signals and alarm/key fob | 
| Advertised ready-to-ride weight | Approximately 155 pounds | 
Sources: Onyx model and pricing overview, RCR product page, RCR feature page and Onyx’s brake and wheel description.
Street, Dual Sport and getting it home
The Street and Dual Sport share the advertised motor and battery ratings. Their clearest hardware differences are the tires and fenders: Street has 4-inch street tires with optional fenders; Dual Sport has 4.5-inch tires with a more aggressive tread and fenders included. (See how the models compare at Onyx.)
Neither arrives like a lightweight bicycle. The RCR is a heavy freight delivery that still needs final assembly, and I wouldn’t recommend unpacking it alone. At roughly 155 pounds ready to ride, it also demands some thought about storage before you order.
I live in a three-flight walk-up. That matters more to my daily experience than another few miles per hour at the top end.
Yes, the RCR has pedals. I doubt many people are spending nearly $5,000 because they’re looking forward to using them.
Small bike, serious performance
I’m 6 feet tall, around 260 pounds and usually carrying a backpack. The RCR has had no trouble moving me around.
Most of my riding has been between 15 and 35 mph, with plenty of time in Normal. I haven’t often felt the need for more. What I appreciate is the reserve power for acceleration and hills, rather than having to ask the bike for everything just to carry a heavier rider.
Seward made a similar point when we talked about the RCR’s development around San Francisco. Steep hills help explain why usable power matters beyond a top-speed claim.
His background also helps explain the bike. An industrial designer whose portfolio includes projects for Sonos and Bird, Seward founded Onyx to bring classic motorbike character to an electric machine. 
He described a combination of motorcycle performance and BMX-style maneuverability. I grew up racing BMX, and I can relate to that influence. The RCR’s compact dimensions make it easy to move around underneath me and maneuver in tighter spaces. Its size is part of its appeal, although the weight is a reminder that this is a very different machine from a BMX bike.
“It’s like a blank canvas that you can customize… It’s not a BMX at all, but it definitely has some influence from when I was a kid,” says Seward.
The throttle changes the experience
With this much power, how it arrives matters.
On my test bike, Eco and Normal feel smoother and more forgiving. Sport and Hyper respond more immediately to wrist movement. Switching modes changes more than the available speed; it changes how carefully I need to feed in the throttle.
I like having that choice. Sometimes I want an easy cruise. Other times, I appreciate a quicker response. A gentler mode doesn’t eliminate the need for careful throttle control, but it makes the bike’s delivery better suited to how I want to ride.
These impressions apply to the software on my test bike. They aren’t a comparison of Onyx’s newer Cruise and Thrill tunes.
What I can say about range
I haven’t completed a controlled range test, so I don’t have a measured full-charge figure to give you.
What I do have is several hundred miles of use without range anxiety. On one ride from around 151st Street in Harlem to East 26th Street, the display showed a drop of about nine percentage points. My ride took me through Central Park, so we’re looking at about 9 miles. After longer outings through Queens and Brooklyn, I’ve returned with roughly 60% to 70% of the indicated charge remaining.
My much lighter teenage son also rode the RCR on an outing through those boroughs. I recall the indicated charge dropping by 17%, although that wasn’t a controlled comparison with my own riding.
One thing that continues to impress me about the Onyx RCR 80V is just how quiet its motor is. There’s none of that high-pitched whining or wheezing you sometimes hear from electric motors. Power delivery is equally impressive, remaining smooth and consistent whether I’m accelerating from a standstill or riding at higher speeds. I’ve also noticed how much the route itself can affect battery consumption. On a recent commute from 151st Street to East 26th Street, I took a different route instead of traveling entirely through Central Park and used just 6% of the battery compared with 9% on a previous ride. It’s a good reminder that real-world range isn’t simply about distance. Terrain, elevation changes, traffic, speed and riding conditions all influence how efficiently the bike uses energy.
Those readings describe what I saw on the display. They don’t establish that each percentage point equals a mile, or that the bike will travel 100 miles on a charge. Without recorded distances, consistent conditions and a fuller discharge test, that would be an extrapolation.
Rider weight, speed, acceleration and terrain all matter. My conclusion is narrower: the battery has comfortably covered the rides I’ve taken. Someone spending more time at high speed should expect a different experience.
Onyx itself recommends watching battery voltage for a better indication of remaining charge and range. That’s another reason to treat my percentage readings as observations rather than precision measurements. (Here’s Onyx’s battery guidance.)
Comfortable suspension, with limits at the seat
The RCR fits me surprisingly well, and the suspension has done a good job taking the edge off New York’s potholes and broken pavement.
The seat is comfortable with good cushioning for shorter rides. After about 90 minutes, though, I start shifting around. The suspension helps with the road underneath me, but it doesn’t eliminate the discomfort that builds during a longer ride. That also could be due to my size; I’m far from a lightweight.
The brakes have also felt consistently strong. After a few hundred miles, lever travel still feels close to how it did at the start, and I haven’t noticed a meaningful decline in stopping performance. That’s a riding impression, not a measured stopping-distance or brake-wear test.
Cruise control and reverse were pleasant surprises
Cruise control sounded like a minor convenience until I used it. On the inclines I’ve encountered with it engaged, the RCR has held the selected speed even with my weight aboard. That has been a more useful demonstration of its available power than a top-speed run.
Discovering that it could also reverse was another pleasant surprise. On a machine this heavy, powered reverse is a feature I’m glad to have. Onyx documents both functions in its advanced controls guide.
CarPlay is a favorite feature — and a frustration
I didn’t expect to care this much about CarPlay. Having navigation and audio controls on the built-in display means I can leave my phone put away.
My main complaint is what happens to the motorbike’s own information. While using CarPlay, especially during a call, I want speed and battery status to remain easy to see. On my test bike, they aren’t presented as conveniently as I’d like.
Onyx told me it intends to address the display issue through a software update.
Navigation brings up another issue. I’d like routing that better reflects the vehicle I’m riding. Because it uses CarPlay, it offers driving directions. However, I would like the option to choose a different route if I choose to.
“Having Android Auto and CarPlay in the bike makes me want to ride more … Part of the new update will show stats like battery level and mode on the side while using it,” says Seward, who is also Onyx’s chief design officer.
Signals, lights and wet pavement
The turn signals sit close to the body, with less protruding hardware to catch on something. I like that design, but in sunny settings, the signals may not be as visible.
They don’t self-cancel. The display indicators help, but I’d prefer automatic cancellation to discovering I’ve announced a left turn for the last 20 blocks (a minor complaint). The Bluetooth connection indicator is another small, useful display detail.
The headlight has worked well for the nighttime riding I’ve done. The halo running light and main beam give the bike a distinctive look, with high beam available when needed.
I’ve also ridden in the rain and on wet pavement without noticing handling problems. That’s limited experience, not a comprehensive wet-weather test. The more immediate issue is spray, as my bike doesn’t have the optional fenders installed, and New York street water gets everywhere.
Fenders are high on my list before doing more wet-weather riding.
Tubeless tires and everyday maintenance
The tubeless setup matters to me because removing a motorized rear wheel to deal with a flat tube can become a project. I’d rather avoid that extra complication where possible.
Tubeless doesn’t mean puncture-proof, and I wouldn’t assume any roadside plug is a permanent repair suitable for motorcycle speeds. But it’s a great go-to when in a pinch. Not having to remove the wheel to make it to your destination is clutch.
“These are basically motorcycle wheels and tires, so if you get a nail, you can patch or plug it without taking the wheel off and replacing the whole tube,” says Seward.
Forget the fob and the bike stays put
I’ve kept the RCR in storage at my partner’s apartment because she has an elevator. I sometimes forget to leave the key fob with it, which works well until I arrive without the fob.
That experience made phone or NFC access more appealing. Seward told me Onyx is developing app-based diagnostics, firmware updates and service support, and we discussed possible phone access. I’d welcome it, along with integrated tracking or movement alerts.
For now, I keep an AirTag hidden in the bike. I’ve also found the rear-wheel locking behavior reassuring when the bike is secured, although that isn’t a substitute for a physical lock.
Onyx already links a Superpower BMS app for battery monitoring. That should be distinguished from the broader app and unlocking features we discussed; I haven’t established that those proposed functions are available. (See the Onyx product page.)
The pedals don’t settle the legal question
I think of the RCR as a compact electric motorcycle. That description doesn’t, by itself, establish whether a particular example can be registered for road use. But it can be insured.
New York’s legal definition of an electric-assist bicycle includes a motor below 750 watts and specified assistance-speed limits. The RCR’s advertised power and performance exceed those limits. Buyers shouldn’t assume that pedals or a lower-speed setting make it a legal e-bike. (See New York’s DMV definitions.)
I haven’t verified New York registration eligibility for this exact model and configuration. That needs to be resolved with the DMV and the manufacturer before it can be presented as a straightforward street-legal commuting option. Bicycle lanes and walking routes should not be assumed available to it.
Beyond the ride: A conversation with Tim Seward
Seward’s explanation of Onyx starts with the products he no longer wanted to design. During our conversation, he described working on consumer electronics for brands including Sonos, HP and Samsung, only to watch products become disposable shortly after reaching the market. His experiences with furniture and old gas-powered mopeds suggested a different approach.
The following excerpts are edited for length and clarity from the interview transcript. Questions have been shortened, and the discussion has been reordered by topic. Future features are plans described during the interview, not confirmation that they are available today.
CNET: Is there anything about your background or the bike that people might not know?
Seward: Before Onyx, I was a big consumer-electronics designer. I worked on Sonos, HP, Samsung, and all sorts of products you would see at Best Buy. While I liked that job, I didn’t like that people were throwing away their products.
When I was customizing gas-powered mopeds, I realized I was working on vehicles 30 to 50 years old. Who knows how many hands it went through until it got to me? I was like, I need to make products like this. I need to make products that, even if Onyx dies tomorrow, the products will live on. I didn’t want to continue to create landfill.
If an owner keeps this bike for five years, what can they realistically expect for battery health?
With our extra layer of health protections, we are confident our battery pack will show only a 10% degradation in 10 years. So, at the five-year mark, you won’t even notice much of a difference, if any, in performance.
(That’s an ambitious prediction. Seward’s response didn’t include the testing, charging habits or usage conditions behind it, so I wouldn’t treat it as a guaranteed outcome or a warranty. It does give me something specific to follow up on as the bike ages.)
How committed is Onyx to supporting owners with replacement parts years down the road?
We strive to offer hard-to-find parts even for discontinued products that are 5 to 6 years old. Also, our newest model, the RCR 80V, uses many parts that are compatible with aftermarket upgrades, so you can modify or maintain it for decades to come.
(That gets to one of my biggest questions about an expensive electric vehicle: What happens when something breaks after the model is no longer current? Aftermarket compatibility could help keep the RCR running, although it isn’t a guarantee that every component will remain available.)
What sets Onyx apart from the growing number of electric motorcycle companies?
We are not just building a bike. We are building a community of riders who support each other across the globe.
(That connects with how I found my way to Onyx. I met John Angel while testing another bike, and he kept encouraging me to try an RCR. Before I spoke with the company, another rider had already shared his experience and got me interested.
The community side matters most when it becomes useful: Someone helping you understand a feature, troubleshoot a problem or figure out a modification. That’s the kind of owner involvement I’d like to see continue as Onyx grows.
Onyx also brings its community together through events like Onyx Week, where owners and enthusiasts participate in organized rides, meet members of the Onyx team, exchange ideas, and connect with other riders. Events have been organized in Los Angeles and New York, giving owners an opportunity to experience the community beyond online discussions and social media.)
What stays with me
The RCR has more power than I usually need and has covered my outings without battery anxiety. CarPlay and cruise control have become features I actually value. The seat can become less comfortable on longer rides, and the display should show the current speed and battery level while on a call.
Talking with Seward gave me a clearer understanding of the decisions behind those experiences. Customer feedback helped shape the 80V, while his experience with disposable electronics explains why he wants owners to keep these bikes running.
It’s nice to hear a company talk about making something you can keep for years instead of pushing you to buy a new model every year. That intention still has to be backed by replacement parts, documentation and service. Onyx’s published guidance says it doesn’t repair, refurbish or rebalance batteries, so long-term battery support remains an important question. (See Onyx’s battery support policy.)
For me, that’s what makes this worth looking at beyond the review — understanding why the RCR was built this way, how owners influence what comes next and whether the support can live up to the design. Would I recommend getting one? Heck yeah!
results.summary:
The Onyx RCR 80V is a high-performance electric motorbike that blends BMX-inspired maneuverability with modern features like Apple CarPlay, offering a customizable platform for urban commuters and enthusiasts.

### Key Points
- The RCR 80V features an 8kW nominal rear hub motor, a removable 3.6kWh battery, and a claimed top speed of 65–75 mph.
- Performance metrics include a 0–30 mph acceleration time of 1.7 seconds and a claimed maximum range of 140 miles under optimal conditions.
- The bike weighs approximately 155 pounds and is available in Street and Dual Sport configurations, differing primarily in tire tread and fender inclusion.
- Integrated technology includes a TFT touchscreen, cruise control, regenerative braking, and Apple CarPlay/Android Auto connectivity.
- Onyx emphasizes long-term repairability and aftermarket compatibility, aiming to avoid the "disposable" product cycle common in consumer electronics.

### Why it Matters
The Onyx RCR 80V represents a shift toward durable, modular electric mobility that prioritizes owner customization and long-term maintenance over planned obsolescence. For consumers, this approach offers a compelling alternative to disposable tech, though potential buyers must carefully navigate the complex legal and registration requirements associated with its high-performance capabilities.

results.title: Hackers Breach Enterprise Firewalls and VPNs, Exposing Over 70,000 Credentials
results.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
results.content:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a large-scale campaign that has targeted exposed network edge devices such as Fortinet FortiGate and Palo Alto Networks GlobalProtect firewalls.
"Artifacts from this investigation also indicate that operators in this campaign have obtained access to numerous organizations worldwide, and have attempted to further compromise some victims, resulting in persistent remote access and data exfiltration," according to a joint investigation published by Group-IB and NyxLab.
The widespread exploitation activity has been attributed to a threat actor known as k0t, who also goes by the aliases CryptoFeel, Member19, and QazWsxShop. The cybercriminal actor was first seen in the wild on October 22, 2025.
The threat actor is assessed to share connections with ransomware groups such as Qilin and The Gentlemen, likely operating as an initial access broker or an affiliate. Analysis of the threat actor's dark web activity reveals a keen interest in purchasing vulnerability exploit code and tools or premium accounts for metadata search engines like FOFA and ZoomEye.
The campaign's victims are global and belong to a broad range of sectors, given the indiscriminate targeting of exposed network devices. A significant chunk of compromises are said to have taken place between February and June 2026, which also overlaps with another credential harvesting campaign codenamed FortiBleed.
Nearly 38% of victims are concentrated in the Asia Pacific region, followed by 31.9% in Latin America, 15.8% in Europe, and 12.7% in the Middle East and North Africa.
The attack chain plays out as follows -
- Conduct reconnaissance through public scanning tools like FOFA and ZoomEye to enumerate internet-facing VPN and firewall appliances, filter candidates by product, and put together target lists of potentially vulnerable edge devices.
- Attempt to exploit these devices via known vulnerabilities like CVE-2025-64446 (a path traversal flaw in FortiWeb) and CVE-2026-0257 (an authentication bypass flaw in Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS and Prisma Access) through bespoke Python scripts named "fortnew.py" and "exploit_2026_0257.py," or perform brute-force attacks using common username and password combinations, to obtain initial access.
- Establish a foothold on the targets via an OpenConnect VPN connection.
- Conduct post-exploitation actions and additional credential theft like enumeration of Active Directory, SMB, and installed antivirus solution.
- Establish persistence on the host via legitimate remote access tools like MeshCentral Agent, Atera, Teramind, and AnyDes, as well as an open-source, adversary-emulation framework known as AdaptixC2.
- Exfiltrate harvested data using Rclone into Wasabi S3 buckets and MEGA cloud drives.
The attacks are also characterized by the use of legitimate administrator and pentesting utilities like NetExec, SoftPerfect, Impacket, noPac, Kerbrute, PetitPotam, and Mimikatz to burrow deeper into victims' corporate environments.
"k0t appears to select potential targets by enumerating exposed network appliances at scale rather than researching individual organizations," Group-IB and NyxLab researchers said. "His stated geographic priorities begin with the United States and Canada, followed by European countries and selected APAC markets."
"The product and location of an exposed device therefore appear to matter more than the industry of the organization operating it, consistent with the broad range of victims observed in this campaign."
k0t's links to Qilin and The Gentlemen stem from the fact that many victims of the campaign were also later listed by the ransomware groups on their data leak sites. However, the exact nature of the connection between the threat and these gangs is unclear.
What's more, Group-IB and NyxLab said they found a "negligible overlap" in compromised data between this activity and FortBleed. More than 70,000 exposed credentials associated with network devices and LDAP dumps have been identified in connection with the campaign.
"This aligns with reports that many operators are likely to be involved in the FortiBleed activity cluster, suggesting that this may be a separate dataset, operator subset, or related access operation within the broader FortiBleed-related activity," the researchers said. "Organizations are advised to act on ensuring that any vulnerabilities mentioned in this report are appropriately remedied."
results.summary:
Cybersecurity researchers have identified a widespread campaign by the threat actor k0t targeting exposed network edge devices, including Fortinet and Palo Alto Networks firewalls, to facilitate data exfiltration.

### Key Points
- Threat actor k0t, also known as CryptoFeel, has compromised global organizations by exploiting vulnerabilities like CVE-2025-64446 and CVE-2026-0257.
- The campaign utilizes reconnaissance tools like FOFA and ZoomEye to identify vulnerable VPN and firewall appliances for initial access.
- Attackers establish persistence using legitimate remote management software such as MeshCentral, Atera, and the AdaptixC2 framework.
- Stolen data is exfiltrated to Wasabi S3 buckets and MEGA cloud drives, with over 70,000 credentials identified in connection with the activity.
- Victims are geographically diverse, with the highest concentrations located in the Asia Pacific region at 38% and Latin America at 31.9%.
- The actor maintains suspected ties to ransomware groups Qilin and The Gentlemen, likely acting as an initial access broker.

### Why it Matters
This campaign highlights the significant risk posed by internet-facing network appliances that remain unpatched or improperly secured against known vulnerabilities. By acting as an initial access broker for ransomware gangs, these attackers provide a critical entry point that can lead to widespread corporate data breaches and operational disruption.

results.title: Inside the LiteLLM 1.107.0 supply chain compromise: Credential theft through Python startup hooks
results.author: Microsoft Security Research, Mahesh Mandava, Srinivasan Govindarajan, Sagar Patil and Suriyaraj Natarajan
results.content:
On October 21, 2026, a compromised LiteLLM 1.107.0 release was published to the Python Package Index (PyPI) and distributed through official container images. The malicious package added files that Python could execute during normal interpreter initialization. An application did not need to import LiteLLM for the payload to run: starting Python in an affected environment could be enough.
Microsoft analyzed two execution paths in the affected wheels: a credential collector launched through a path extension, and a Unix-oriented loader persisted through site-specific configuration. The collector targeted authentication material across developer tools, AI applications, cloud environments, browsers, and infrastructure. A separate database module attempted to read selected credential and model-configuration records from the LiteLLM proxy.
Endpoint observations on Windows and macOS matched the recovered collector’s discovery, encryption, and outbound-connection behavior. In one Windows example, a routine Python invocation to install an unrelated dependency activated the collector. This distinction matters for response: investigators should not start Python or pip inside a suspect environment to determine whether the malicious package is present.
This blog explains the startup mechanisms, the credentials the payload could reach, and the evidence defenders can use to investigate exposure. It also provides Microsoft Defender detection information, advanced hunting queries, and recovery guidance. Removing the package or a release tag is not sufficient recovery. Organizations must address the affected Python environment, any surviving processes, and credentials accessible to the compromised identity.
Attack overview
LiteLLM is commonly deployed as a gateway between applications and model providers. In that position it may have access to model-provider API keys, database connection strings, workload identities, routing configuration, and tenant policy data. The same package is also used on developer workstations, build agents, test systems, and containers, which widened the set of environments that could be exposed by the compromised release.
According to LiteLLM maintainers, stolen developer GitHub credentials were used to alter the release workflow and redirect it to the lookalike repository Berri-AI/litellm rather than the legitimate BerriAI/litellm repository. A credential associated with another developer account was then used to satisfy a production approval step. Microsoft has not independently determined how the attacker first accessed the upstream environment or obtained those credentials.
The compromised package used Python startup mechanisms to execute malicious code automatically, meaning exposure was not limited to systems actively using a LiteLLM gateway. Developer workstations, continuous integration and continuous delivery/deployment (CI/CD) agents, test environments, containers, and other systems that started Python with the affected package installed could also execute the payload. The malicious code supported credential collection and, on Unix-based systems, retrieval and execution of additional Python code.
1. Compromised package distribution
The compromised LiteLLM 1.107.0 release delivered malicious Python startup files to environments where the package was installed.
2. Automatic payload execution
Python startup processing launched the credential collector without requiring the application to actively use LiteLLM gateway functionality.
3. Credential and sensitive-data collection
The collector targeted developer credentials, cloud credentials, browser data, SSH material, environment variables, and LiteLLM database data accessible to the affected process.
4. Encryption and exfiltration
Collected data was encrypted and transmitted to an attacker-controlled endpoint.
5. Conditional retrieval and execution of additional code
On Unix-based systems, the payload supported retrieving and executing additional Python code, although this activity was not confirmed.
Technical details
Compromised package distribution and automatic payload execution
The compromised wheel packaged cook.pth, cook.py, and sitecustomize.py under litellm-1.107.0.data/purelib/. During installation, these files were relocated into the Python environment’s library directory, outside the normal litellm application directory. This placement enabled execution through Python’s normal site initialization, which processes executable import statements in .pth files and later attempts to import the sitecustomize module.
The first execution path began with the single executable line in cook.pth: “import cook”. This loaded cook.py, whose wrapper Base64-decoded and zlib-decompressed an embedded Python program before executing the recovered source. The program identified itself as PRIVCOLLECT and performed credential collection in a daemon thread.
Before starting the thread, the collector checked the inherited PRIVCOLLECT_ACTIVE environment variable. A nonempty value caused it to return; otherwise, it set the flag, limiting duplicate collection in descendant processes. After an upload returned HTTP 200, it attempted to write /tmp/.pc_once_72129118c59f5636c0bb. These duplicate-suppression gates were not containment controls: startup alone did not prove collection or upload completed, because a short-lived process could exit before the thread finished, while write failures or temporary-storage changes could leave the marker absent.
A second startup mechanism used sitecustomize.py, providing a separate Unix-oriented execution path with an embedded collector and functionality to retrieve and execute additional Python code from a remote host. Remote retrieval and execution through this path were not confirmed.
Together, these mechanisms extended potential exposure beyond active LiteLLM deployments: simply starting Python in an affected environment could activate the malicious code, even when LiteLLM itself was never imported. Because the startup files resided outside the litellm application directory, removing only the application files could leave the malicious startup components behind.
Credential and sensitive-data collection
The recovered collector was designed to gather sensitive authentication material across developer tools, AI applications, cloud environments, browsers, and infrastructure. It runs multiple collection modules sequentially with independent error handling, allowing collection to continue even when individual targets are unavailable or inaccessible.
| Target | Recovered collection behavior | 
| Developer and AI tools | Reads selected authentication and configuration files for AI assistants, integrated development environments (IDEs) , GitHub Copilot, VS Code, and MCP integrations. Collects fixed paths and top-level JSON files in selected tool directories under a collection budget. | 
| Source control and package ecosystems | Searches Git credentials, package-manager configuration, selected dotenv files, and private-key extensions. Shallow directory walks and file-size limits constrain these searches. | 
| Cloud and workload credentials | Reads AWS, Azure CLI, and Google Cloud configuration or credential caches; Kubernetes service-account files; Docker configuration; and mounted secrets. It also attempts AWS and GCP metadata credential retrieval. | 
| Browsers and user histories | Accesses Chromium-family and Firefox credential-related data and browsing history, plus shell, database-client, and interactive-tool histories. Password decryption is platform- and format-dependent. | 
| Process environments | Collects its own environment and, on Linux, other process environments readable through procfs. This can expose secrets beyond variables explicitly configured for the LiteLLM process. | 
| Private keys and infrastructure | Targets readable Secure Shell (SSH) material and selected GNU Privacy Guard (GPG), Transport Layor Security (TLS), CI/CD, Vault, and infrastructure-tool configuration. A target appearing in the code does not establish successful access. | 
| LiteLLM proxy data | When its prerequisites are satisfied, starts a Python child using Prisma to read selected fields from two proxy database tables, with a 500-row limit for each query | 
Encryption and exfiltration
After collection, the payload serializes module results and host metadata as JSON. Each run generates a 32-byte AES key and a 16-byte initialization vector. AES-256-CBC encrypts the collection document; an embedded 4,096-bit RSA public key wraps the AES key using OAEP. The OpenSSL path tries SHA-256 and then SHA-1 for OAEP, and the resulting metadata records the selected digest.
The collector places three members in a gzip-compressed tar archive: data.bin, containing the initialization vector (IV) and encrypted collection; key.bin, containing the wrapped AES key; and hdr.json, containing plaintext envelope metadata. It then attempts an HTTP POST to hxxp://www[.]litellm[.]dev/healthcheck, using application/octet-stream, a fixed browser-like User-Agent, and a body checksum in an X-SHA256 header. The upload routine retries and treats only HTTP 200 as success.
The OpenSSL backend creates temporary directories beginning with .pc_e_, stages input and output files and removes them after use.
Conditional retrieval and execution of additional code
In addition to the credential collector, the compromised package contained a separate Unix-oriented loader in sitecustomize.py, designed to retrieve and execute additional Python code. When Python starts, the loader takes an exclusive lock on /tmp/remote_code_loader.lock so that only one instance runs per host and detaches into the background. Each cycle reads a GitHub-hosted domain.txt file, which acts as a mutable pointer to an attacker-controlled server.
If a valid server address is returned and successfully resolved, the loader is designed to request /codepy from that server, compile the returned content, and execute it as Python code within the affected environment. This gives the attacker a mechanism to change the second-stage payload without publishing another compromised LiteLLM package. This loader is separate from the credential collector delivered directly in the compromised package.
At the time the cited researchers examined domain.txt, it was empty and no second-stage retrieval or execution was confirmed. Because the file could be changed, the loader remained a re-armable remote-code execution mechanism.
Mitigation and protection guidance
Microsoft recommends the following actions for organizations that installed, mirrored, or built images with LiteLLM 1.107.0:
- Find and contain every affected copy. Identify LiteLLM 1.107.0 across installed environments, uv and pip caches, internal package mirrors, lock files, build outputs, and container images. Scope mutable container tags and the relevant exposure windows once validated and compare artifacts with the customer-ready hashes in the indicators of compromise section. For background, see secure software supply chain practices and Docker image digests. Digests are preferable to mutable tags because they identify immutable image content.
- Prevent Python execution and investigate from outside the environment. Isolate affected developer workstations, build agents, test systems, containers, and AI gateway hosts. Where operationally safe, stop running Python processes and prevent automation from restarting them. Do not run python, pip, or other commands that invoke the affected interpreter during evidence collection; inspect the environment with trusted tools from a known-clean system. Python normally processes site configuration, including executable import lines in .pth files, during initialization.
- Rebuild from verified artifacts. Confirm that cook.pth, cook.py, and sitecustomize.py were removed from the environment library path. Rebuilding is more reliable than assuming that deleting the litellm directory cleaned the top-level startup files.
- Rotate reachable credentials from a known-clean machine. Include model-provider keys, cloud and workload credentials, CI/CD secrets, source-control and registry tokens, SSH and GPG keys, AI coding-tool tokens, and browser sessions available to the affected identity. On proxy hosts, include stored provider credentials and DATABASE_URL. Revoke affected identity sessions rather than assuming password or key rotation immediately invalidates every active token or application session. See revoke user access in Microsoft Entra ID.
- Correlate before declaring compromise. Combine file hashes, Python process ancestry, .pc_e_ cryptographic staging, network destination, workload identity, and subsequent cloud or identity use. Do not use package presence or a generic filename as the sole verdict.
- Strengthen dependency controls. Use hash-pinned lock files, verify package and image provenance, use container digests instead of floating tags, and admit packages to internal mirrors only after review. See best practices for a secure software supply chain and dependency scanning in Azure DevOps.
- Restrict outbound access. Developer workstations, build agents, test systems, containers, and AI gateway hosts should not have unrestricted outbound HTTP access unless required. Route outbound traffic through managed egress controls, deny unnecessary destinations, and allowlist required services. See control outbound internet access from Azure.
- Enable Microsoft Defender for Endpoint protections. Onboard supported developer workstations, build agents, and AI gateway servers to Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, and enable Microsoft Defender Antivirus real-time and cloud-delivered protection where supported. See configure always-on protection and configure cloud protection.

results.summary:
The October 21, 2026, release of LiteLLM version 1.107.0 was compromised to include malicious code that automatically executes upon Python interpreter initialization, threatening developer and cloud environments.

### Key Points
- Attackers compromised the LiteLLM 1.107.0 release on PyPI by hijacking developer GitHub credentials to redirect the workflow to a malicious repository.
- The malicious package uses Python startup hooks, such as `.pth` and `sitecustomize.py` files, to execute a credential collector without requiring the application to be imported.
- The payload targets sensitive data including cloud credentials, SSH keys, browser history, environment variables, and AI-related configuration files.
- Collected data is encrypted using AES-256-CBC and RSA, then exfiltrated to an attacker-controlled domain via HTTP POST requests.
- Unix-based systems were also exposed to a secondary loader capable of retrieving and executing additional remote Python code.
- Microsoft advises organizations to rotate all potentially exposed credentials and rebuild environments from verified, clean artifacts rather than simply deleting the package.

### Why it Matters
This incident highlights a critical supply chain vulnerability where malicious code executes automatically during standard Python environment initialization, bypassing typical application-level security controls. Because the payload targets high-value credentials across developer workstations and CI/CD pipelines, organizations must treat all systems that installed the affected package as potentially compromised.

results.title: Can presidents affect gas prices?
results.author: Georgia Tech
results.content:
Economists have long dismissed the public perception that presidents influence gas prices as economic illiteracy, but new research calls that assumption into question.
The research finds significant differences in average gas prices across administrations.
The study is timely, arriving amid widespread public discontent over rising fuel prices, with voter frustrations reflected in a series of national polls blaming the Trump administration.
Although the researchers do not determine how much of the price differences across administrations, if any, are caused by presidents themselves, they argue economists may have been too confident in dismissing the possibility without much direct evidence.
“Even though it’s a topic of immense public interest, we found almost no literature on the question and it seems like it’s been unduly ignored,” says Matthew Oliver, a professor in Georgia Tech’s School of Economics in the Ivan Allen College of Liberal Arts.
He points to the gap in perception between energy experts and non-experts as a potential culprit. In fact, this work was inspired by “I did that” stickers he saw on gas pumps in 2022, with an image of then-President Joe Biden pointing at the 20-year-high gas prices.
“I scoffed at the idea that the president can influence the retail price of gasoline, and I don’t think I’m unique in that regard amongst my colleagues,” Oliver says. “So that leads me to believe that a big reason why this has never been researched thoroughly by economists is that we thought we already knew the answer to this question.”
But the work opens it back up to inquiry, and they encourage more research to determine which mechanisms are actually driving these changing prices.
“The more that you dig into it, based on the literature that exists in economics and studying things like the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, the more it’s clear that there are actually more reasons to think that the president can influence fuel prices than not,” says Dylan Brewer, an associate professor in the School.
To explore the issue, Brewer and Oliver looked at both public opinion and real-world fuel-price data. For their paper, published in Energy Economics, they commissioned a nationally representative survey of 1,018 US residents and 216 professional economists.
The results showed that 57.1% of energy experts surveyed believed the president had no or very little influence over retail gas prices, a viewpoint the authors also shared. In contrast, more than two-thirds of non-experts believed the president has a moderate or strong influence over gas prices.
So, the researchers analyzed 19 years of weekly fuel-price data in the US, Canada, Great Britain, and France to determine if the public was observing a real phenomenon. They found that:
- Average gas prices change under presidents: Average gas prices often differed significantly under different US presidents between 2003 and 2022.
- The same pattern is seen abroad: Average gas prices also changed between many administrations in France, Great Britain, and Canada.
- These patterns remained even when controlling for factors such as crude oil prices, fuel taxes, economic downturns, and major international events like pandemics or war that can affect energy markets.
- However, the researchers did not claim to establish a causal link between the president and gas prices because too many additional variables are involved.
- The paper shows that Americans may believe this common media narrative because gas prices and presidential administrations are correlated.
The study doesn’t find price differences between every administration, but does document a pattern of changes across administrations in multiple countries. For example, in Canada, gasoline prices were about 47 cents per gallon lower under Prime Minister Mark Carney than under his predecessor, Justin Trudeau. In the United Kingdom, gasoline prices were about 55 cents per gallon lower under former Prime Minister Theresa May than under David Cameron, who led the UK government before her.
In one US comparison, gasoline prices were about 39 cents per gallon higher in the early years of President Barack Obama’s administration than during the final years of President George W. Bush’s presidency.
“In a very simple statistical sense, if you look at fuel prices during different presidential regimes under sets of controls, there are different fuel prices across presidents. And we can’t say that that’s because any president caused those changes, but the fact is that the prices are different across presidents,” Brewer says.
“So if economists really think that the president doesn’t have influence, the burden of proof is on economists to explain that these differences can’t be interpreted as the result of each president’s actions.”
Whether or not presidents actually affect gas prices, many people believe they do, and that’s enough to drive behavior in important ways, Oliver says.
As diesel prices hit record highs in the United States—with unleaded gas prices not far behind—polls show many Americans blame President Trump for the recent rise in gas prices, and perceive the Democratic Party as better equipped to address the issue. With midterm elections looming, these perceptions can have consequences at the polls.
“This question is highly important to almost everyone, so much so that it moves entire elections,” he says. “It drives economic activity; it’s a litmus test for how the overall economy is doing at any given point in time. So, the motivation is to engage the public and try to arm people with better information about these debates when they go on in the public sphere.”
For instance, people in America link presidents and gas prices much more strongly when gas prices rise than when they fall. Brewer and Oliver found that for every dollar per gallon that gas prices go up, Google searches such as “Trump gas prices” or “Biden gas prices” jump about 53 percentage points. However, when gas prices fall by one dollar, searches don’t change by a statistically significant amount.
“The discourse from the side of the experts needs to take this question more seriously, but I would say the same for the average political commentator’s discourse as well, because they also assume and promote the idea that presidents can influence these prices,” Brewer says. “But it’s just not that clear. Both sides are relatively confident, and the discourse should be a little bit more cautious.”
More featured research from the School of Economics: Does Wildfire Smoke Affect the Economy?
What’s Next?
Brewer and Oliver say more research is needed to establish or rule out a causal link between presidential policies and gas prices. Variables that clouded their analysis included long policy lag times, the fact that one leader inherits conditions created by previous leaders, the possibility that fuel prices themselves help determine who gets elected, and the many overlapping economic, political, and market forces that influence prices at the same time.
Rather than settling the debate, the researchers hope the paper encourages others to investigate the issue further, devising ways to better understand if there’s a relationship, and if so, how it works.
“I think what we are hoping is to start a new strand of literature, if you will, where economists and energy policy experts and analysts would be studying this question a little bit more deeply,” Oliver says.
Source: Georgia Tech

- Authors Matthew Oliver and Dylan Brewer emphasize that while a correlation exists, they have not yet established a direct causal link between presidential policy and prices.

Public perception regarding presidential influence on fuel costs significantly impacts voter behavior and election outcomes, yet the topic has been largely ignored by academic economists. This research highlights a critical disconnect between expert consensus and public belief, suggesting that more rigorous study is required to understand the complex drivers of energy markets.

results.title: Live updates: Bitcoin holds above $81,000 as the AI rout fades and oil climbs
results.author: Shaurya Malwa
results.content:
Bitcoin dipped to about $81,000 late Thursday and has since spent the day boxed in a range of less than $1,000, trading near $81,500 early Friday. After a week of $3,000 swings, it’s the calmest stretch bitcoin has had in days.
It’s down 0.4% over 24 hours and still sits below $82,500, the support it lost on Thursday.
Altcoins were mixed. BNB was the standout, up nearly 2% to about $745, and DOGE added about 1%. XMR gave back part of Thursday’s jump, falling 7% to about $607, and ZEC lost nearly 4% to about $1,200. HYPE, XRP, ether and SOL slipped about 1% or less, with ether just under $2,400, according to CoinDesk data.
Stocks found their footing too. Nasdaq 100 futures were little changed after the index’s worst day since June, and an ETF tracking chipmakers edged higher before the open. Meta kept falling, while SpaceX climbed on reports that it plans to become a wireless carrier.
Oil is the worry. Brent crude touched its highest level since early May, which complicates the inflation outlook heading into the Fed’s Oct. 27–28 meeting. Treasuries gave back some of Thursday’s haven rally, which had pushed the 10-year yield down by the most in more than a year. Gold and the dollar were flat.

No bad news today, but the links below are good for several long coffee breaks over the coming weekend. Enjoy!
Part the First: Political Hope in a Time of Despair. Independent media of all types have become essential to understanding our world. There is nothing new about that to this community. Salvation South is always interesting. The founder, Chuck Reece, was present at the creation of The Bitter Southerner, which was the source of our discussion of the lunchroom ladies last February. This week Salvation South takes up Southern Politics in an article by Doug Cumming, who is a retired journalist and journalism professor, in his No Choice in God’s Country.
And “No Choice” it has been for a long time in different parts of Georgia. Most of Rural North Georgia has been deep red for some time. The same is true in South Georgia, except for several very rural counties of the Black Belt. Larger urban areas, including the cities of Atlanta, Macon, Augusta, Athens, and Savannah tend to elect Democrats, but they are surrounded by a deep shade of gerrymander red. More widely in the South:
In Rockbridge County, Virginia, (one of the most beautiful parts of the United States) with its little university town of Lexington, there were always two political parties and competing candidates for the General Assembly in Richmond. But in parts of the Deep South today, counties are so “red” or “blue” that many local candidates for state legislatures face no opposition on Election Day. Uncontested state legislative races are increasingly the norm across the South. A Salvation South analysis of data from Ballotpedia found this: seven states, from South Carolina straight across to Louisiana and Arkansas (also Kentucky, but not Tennessee or Florida), had only one major party on more than half of the ballots for state legislatures in the latest state legislative elections. And those candidates were mostly Republican.
The most extreme examples in 2023 were Louisiana (where 82.6 percent of the seats were uncontested, and 69 percent of those were Republican) and Mississippi (where 86 percent were uncontested, and 67 percent were Republican).
To me, that seems not only undemocratic. It seems immoral.
I have spent much of the past year in rural North Georgia, a break from my retirement in comfortably liberal Decatur. On some Sundays, I sought the William Jamesian “varieties of religious experience” worshipping at different midsized churches. I wasn’t looking for the beating heart of Christian Nationalism or the theology of MAGA. Still, it surprised me that I saw no signs of politics at all.
These were living churches where the Democratic Party had died, and with it, some of the power of the vote. I saw no bumper stickers for candidates in the parking lots. The churches were full, and the gospel was preached. But folks at the coffee hours were too “Christian” to bring up such an uncomfortable subject as politics. They just smiled at the end of that ten-foot pole.
Immoral? When I first voted in Georgia in the mid-term election of 1974, things were the other way around. But like Mr. Cumming, I did feel a sense of participation then, and now. The article never really addresses the nature of our current Uniparty, but that is a national thing. Local and state politics are different and are likely to be the harbinger of change. But I do not think Mr. Cumming should have been surprised that politics did not issue forth from the pulpit or the pews in the churches he visited. For the most part, that is a line that is not crossed, except in mega-churches of uncertain theological provenance.
The Trump signs are scarcer than before. Will dissatisfaction with the Current Administration bring about change? I still pay attention as best I can in a state without even the ghost of the newspaper that used to be delivered daily to each of Georgia’s 159 counties, this is a difficult question. But those candidates who are trying are the proverbial breath of fresh air. Such as Mishael White:
And then there is Mishael White, a Black driver of eighteen-wheelers for Domino’s Pizza who is running for the second time for a state House seat in Henry County, a gateway between Atlanta and middle Georgia. White was encouraged by the Fighting Fifty to run in 2024, when he lost by 14 percentage points to Noelle Kahaian, a Bible-college graduate and paralegal. Kahaian had beat another conservative incumbent in the 2024 Republican primary after crusading against “Critical Race Theory” in the public schools. In the state legislature., she co-sponsored a stalled bill to reduce the authority of the Department of Health and local health boards to require vaccines for infectious diseases.
…
Having moved his family to Georgia from New Orleans after Hurricane Katrina in 2005, Mishael White is campaigning on his ideas to help trade schools (after high school, he got trained in welding at the Avondale Shipyard in New Orleans), to reduce the state’s high maternal mortality rate, and to support small businesses (he owns part of a Stockbridge restaurant, Sheauxtime Kitchen & Lounge).
…
He draws on his experience driving a truck rated for 80,000 pounds gross weight. Driving a big rig, he says, you have to get along and trust fellow drivers, especially when team driving. The predominantly white, MAGA culture becomes irrelevant on the road. And when Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp brags about funding to expand Interstate highways, White says the expansion makes traffic worse. White says the number of big trucks, not the quantity of lanes, is the problem. His solution: more parking areas for trucks so that drivers can choose to drive when fewer cars are out, which truckers would prefer.
In 2024, White lost to Kahaian by 14 percentage points—a 4,717-vote difference. Kamala Harris got 43.3 percent in the district, close to the same as White.
This year, he is running with more wind at his back, and more voters moving into Henry County. The population grew by about 4,400 in 2024, a rate of 1.7 percent a year, according to the U.S. Census Bureau. He doesn’t bring up politics on Sunday mornings at Victory Tabernacle Church International, where he and his family worship. Instead, he is doing interviews and town-hall meetings that end up online. He and his family are knocking on thousands of doors and working the crowds on Saturdays, one of his three days off, in McDonough’s popular Main Street Market.
Less than two weeks to go. We shall see. But a true son of the working class in the Georgia House of Representatives would be a sight to behold! Or as my grandmother, who was a poll worker in the 1930s in Telfair County when dead white people voted in alphabetical order for Governor Gene Talmadge (of Telfair County) in that equally inverted political universe, might have said, “Imagine that!”
Part the Second: Mickey Mantle and Don Larsen in a World Series for the Ages. I am not in general an envious person, but this story elicits some of that feeling in this Little Leaguer who came along about ten years after this adventure. Mickey Mantle was still there, and later I wore #7 on my high school baseball uniform, but it was not the same. The summary of A Picture Perfect World Series, seventy years ago when Don Larsen pitched a perfect game at the end of the season when Mickey Mantle won the Triple Crown (highest batting average, most home runs, and runs batted in):
Seventy years ago this month, a feisty, middle-aged aunt drove two Little Leaguers from Greenville, North Carolina, to New York City for the first time. They left with a photo of Mickey Mantle and memories worthy of a baseball history book.
Enjoy, the shortest read of this Coffee Break!
Part the Third: The Return of Thomas Frank. I have read every book written by Thomas Frank, going back to One Market Under God. Frank was virtually cancelled by the mainstream media for being intelligent. I have ordered his new book, The Creativity Con: How Innovation Became America’s Biggest Racket. The current issue of Jacobin has an excerpt entitled The Creativity Con Ate the Middle Class. Well, something sure did, and I have no doubt Thomas Frank has something worthwhile to say:
The faiths and hopes of the postwar middle-class society have mostly evaporated today. Our parents’ beliefs in consensus and the goodness of American civilization have joined mainline Protestantism and the benevolent corporation on some nostalgia channel of discarded ideas. One signature ideal of that era has survived, however. Indeed, it thrives; it glows with an incandescence that time cannot dim. I am referring to our ongoing fascination with creativity, the human power that our affluent-society ancestors liked to believe made life worth living and that was, at the same time, responsible for the forward motion of civilization itself.
Every year brings a bumper crop of sunny new literature on this tired old subject. Self-help books tell us how to sharpen our skills and be more creative; Substack writers explore the fascinating details of mental performance; South by Southwest (SXSW) and its many imitators bring together practitioners of this colorful art; governments zone urban areas for innovative pursuits; foundations issue sumptuous prizes to the exceptionally creative; executives from industries like advertising and defense assure us of their dedication to the human imagination; and Silicon Valley sells artificial intelligence as a creativity force multiplier — or, rather, it did before we started to fear AI as a creativity poison that would blunt our mental skills if not obsolete them altogether.
The long-running appeal of creativity to middle-class Americans is easy to understand: it is an explanation for progress that seems to put them in history’s starring role. The reason our country is so successful, it assures us, is the day-to-day innovativeness of millions of ordinary but ingenious people. But the actual, real-world effects of creativity have been anything but healthy for the middle-class society. At every step in the long march to our current state of crushing plutocratic inequality, creativity’s holy name was invoked. The big tax cuts of the 1970s and ’80s were done in order to reinvigorate our creativity. Our leaders deregulated banks, did endless favors for tech and pharma, allowed deindustrialization to rust out the heartland, and ushered us generally into a “postindustrial” era in which working people lost their claim on middle-class prosperity — all in order to augment our powers of creativity and innovation.
Yes. A comparison of The Creative Con with We Have Never Been Woke: The Cultural Contradictions of a New Elite, by Musa al-Gharbi, should be worth further discussion one of these days.
Part the Fourth: David W. Orr Is an Island of Sanity in an Insane World. I have read at least six of David W. Orr’s books nine books, and he once even replied to an email from me way back in the day. His students at Oberlin and Arizona State have been a fortunate few, but he has always shared his wisdom with the rest of us. For this part, we return to Front Porch Republic, in a long conversation between Professor Orr and Teddy Macker: The Great Work: An Interview with David W. Orr (NB: ~9,800 words and more than worth the time). A sampling:
With a son-of-a-preacher eloquence; an omnivorous learning; an intelligence alive to connections; a rascally sense of humor; and undeniable soul force, few others have warned us about our nation’s challenges so compellingly as David W. Orr.
We are not living by the terms set by reality for a healthy, lasting tenure on Earth, Orr tells us. We are out of alignment—perilously so—with Creation. We need to immediately “reimagine and remake the human presence on earth in ways that work over the long haul.” To truly heal we need to “stretch our hearts to reach out to other species and future generations.”
Despite the relentlessly unflinching gaze in his many sobering books about the challenges we face (he does not, as he puts it, “understate the problem in order to appear credible”), Orr makes one stouter of heart. Orr does not cynically relish his grim assessments of the global ecological disruption; our ailing democracy; and our “technological somnambulism.” At a time when our country appears to be “haunted by ill angels only” (to borrow from Edgar Allan Poe), Orr calls us to be people of care, compassion, and wisdom; people of thrift, neighborliness, and bravery. We must learn a “patriotism that shifts loyalties from ‘I,’ ‘me,’ and ‘mine’ to ‘we,’ ‘ours,’ and ‘us.’” Instead of being mere voyeurs, scrolling on our phones, we must enter into the breach. “Optimism and pessimism, I think, ought to be put aside,” Orr tells us. “Let’s just buckle down, do what we can, with what’s before us. Everybody has something to offer in this process.”
And Orr encourages us to graduate from what might be called “whole-blindness.” We must become “systems citizens” with a “more capacious view of our obligatedness. “You can’t pull a thread,” Orr says, “without troubling the stars.” Orr’s nine books—which I urge readers to find and read—invite us to reacquaint ourselves with our own agency, nobility, and awareness of “the connections that bind us to each other, to all life, and to all life to come.”
Other writers mentioned include Garrett Hardin, Thomas Berry, Bill McKibben, Wendell Berry, Robert Louis Stevenson, Aldo Leopold, Georgescu-Roegen, Herman Daly, Kate Raworth, Wes Jackson, Jane Austen, Ian McGilchrist, Mary Shelley, Pope Leo XIV, Joseph Wizenbaum, George Orwell…and in the middle:
Even though much of the science is beyond our comprehension, our hope unfortunately still is in better gadgets, not better systems design or improvement of our behavior and the “still unlovely human mind.” And despite the Titanic, Fukushima, and the next “normal accident” waiting in the wings, the hope conceals an even darker reality. Skeptics of technological fundamentalism are today’s heretics, no longer burned at the stake but merely ignored as hopelessly out of touch. We can do better.
As a start, we need shared understandings about our prosthetic devices and the systems in which they are embedded. Here is a very unoriginal list of considerations, adapted from Mary Shelley, Herman Melville, Lewis Mumford, David Ehrenfeld, Neil Postman, David Noble, David Schwartz, Kirkpatrick Sale, among others:
- Using tools, such as hoes, hatchets, shovels, hammers to solve problems, is not a solely human behavior. Some animals do as well. Consider for example how ingeniously birds build their nests with beaks and claws with no opposable thumb and, as far as we know, no engineering degrees. (Or, relatedly, ponder the fact that mere bumblebees have the capacity for inferential reasoning.)
- Every human tool and technological device is embedded in a system of political economy, ecology, culture, and morality.
- Benefits of technology come first, costs later, a pattern elsewhere known as addiction. We can do better.
- The effects of any device, anticipated or not, ripple throughout the larger system with unpredictable consequences.
- Sometimes these effects are counter-intuitive, opposite to what we might logically expect, which is to say they “bite back.”
- Technology amplifies the irony and paradoxes that haunt the human condition. Who coulda known!
- The invention of the process of invention in the nineteenth century made technological innovation a positive feedback system and the rate of change is accelerating.
- Technology-driven improvements often run counter to smarter systems designs that are generally cheaper, faster, and less destructive.
- Technological development without prior and careful public assessment is anti-democratic.
- Finally, is technology a blessing or a curse? In 1972 when asked what he thought of the French Revolution of the 1790s, Chinese Premier Zhou Enlai replied, “It’s too early to say.” So it is with all of our devices and the systems in which they are created and deployed.
Learnedness in every good way whether one agrees or not, unusual for our times. And perhaps not long for our times. But unless we unlearn certain truths our time is coming to an end.
Part the Fifth: The Peace of Wild Things
When despair for the world grows in me
and I wake in the night at the least sound
in fear of what my life and my children’s life might be,
I go and lie down where the wood drake
rests in his beauty on the water, and the great heron feeds.
I come into the peace of wild things
who do not tax their lives with forethought
of grief. I come into the presence of still water.
And I feel above me the day-blind stars
Waiting with their light. For a time
I rest in the grace of the world, and am free.
– Wendell Berry, 1934-2026
Thank you for reading. See you next week. Stay safe out there!

results.content:
Is this the new cyber normal?
The last week has seen a flurry of severe and critical software vulnerabilities affecting thousands of major sites and sending people into a panic. What’s going on here, and what can we do about it?
If we want to understand what’s going on in the world of software security at the moment, we need to understand what’s going on with all these bugs. I’m not a cybersecurity expert, so I’m going to link to external explanations instead of going into the gory technical details myself as these people are always going to do a better job at that.
PHP2Shell – CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (a.k.a. “the big one in the news”)
Two different security teams, one from California security company Calif (as part of OpenAI’s “Patch the Planet” program) and another from Israeli-U.S. cloud security company Wiz (they’re part of Google Cloud, apparently), both found these two Remote Code Execution (RCE) bugs in PHP. They were both using frontier AI models (a.k.a. LLMs, specifically GPT-5.6 Sol/Gemini 4 Argon) to find these vulnerabilities and build the exploits.
Interestingly, one of the bugs (CVE-2026-109618) was found by a security audit the PHP Foundation did in 2024 (funded by the Sovereign Tech Agency which is coincidentally one of the most interesting things happening in the open source space at the moment) but they basically ignored it because they had bigger concerns and couldn’t agree on a fix. The reasoning behind it was that no-one could really figure out how to create an actual exploit based on the theoretical issue.
One thing LLMs are very good at is taking a theoretical security vulnerability, even if that vulnerability is a vague description of what the issue could be, and building it into a full exploit. This has become a major issue in recent months as any notice of a security patch will immediately result in people pointing their LLMs at the codebase, whereupon the agents can very quickly read through diffs until they find something that looks like a security patch, then go backwards to the vulnerability it covers, and follow this all the way to an exploit.
This happens so fast, in fact, that at this point I think it is a reasonable that the moment you announce a security patch should be taken as a last possible date that the full exploit is not being publicly or privately distributed.
This PHP2Shell (as it’s being marketed, vulnerabilities seem to come bundled with their own marketing departments now) is estimated to affect upwards of 70% of the internet, with thousands of websites from Wikimedia Foundation to DeviantArt to much of the UK government and Japanese banking systems to The Traitors BBC programme website. Vulnerabilities do get found, but they don’t normally cause half the internet to shut their servers down, so what’s going on?
To understand this, let’s look at the original post from the PHP Group:
Someone called petecooper posted on Hacker News about the CVEs, apparently unaware that there even was an embargo. This (and other apparent leaks) prompted this hurried statement from the PHP Group and bringing the patch forward from Thursday 22nd to Wednesday 21st. However, the patch still wasn’t going to be available till the next day. This unintentional leak included CVSS scores of 10.0 (i.e. bad, although weirdly the actual scores were 9.2 instead).
Pretty much immediately, this news spread like wildfire and people started panicking. Even though this was found by “responsible security researchers” at “respectable companies”, by the time the security patch actually got released, it was already being exploited in the wild1. The PHP Foundation blamed Calif and a company called Chainguard by saying that Calif leaked a video of the exploit in action (with weird background music and a dancing anime girl) while Chainguard published fixes 6 hours before the embargo was due to lift, both allowing attackers to beat the systems administrators to the punch. The timeline is confusing, but it seems like multiple interconnected things have gone wrong here, all within the space of about 17 hours.
There’s been lots of discussion about whether AI really is the game changer that completely revolutionises computer security or not. The big AI companies (and they are big) obviously want you to think that it is. Some people argue that PHP2Shell is overblown because LLMs tend to be paranoid about vulnerabilities and come up with “exploits” that make bad assumptions (like that the server will run PHP code you upload yourself via some existing file inclusion vulnerability) or cheat in some way. As LiveOverflow points out, LLMs make it very easy to create exploit slop that proves nothing and doesn’t work, but that doesn’t mean that the vulnerability isn’t real and easy to exploit using AI. You can have 10,000 bad slop exploits that don’t work but if there’s one that does, that’s all that matters. Maybe we just need to get used to wading through slop to find the important stuff now.
Others point out that lots of governments (UK2, EU, Japan, USA) got overexcited and released urgent announcements saying everyone had to unplug their computers immediately, so people panicked. I think the reason everyone panicked is that everyone kind of knows that PHP is intensely insecure and they use it anyway, so they’re kind of primed for bad news and to overreact. Also, it actually is really quite bad, so maybe panicking is kind of the correct reaction?
The big takeaway for me from this is that – because of LLMs – the time from “hey I heard there’s a bad RCE in this project” to “there are sophisticated, automated, and concerted attacks using an exploit targeting this vulnerability” has gone from weeks/months to hours/minutes. The fact that there’s loads of non-working exploit slop just shows how genuine expertise is still required to make these things – if you don’t know what you’re looking at, you can’t tell whether the AI has cheated or made bad assumptions.
Links:
- Hacker News: “Tell HN: 2x PHP RCE CVEs with CVSS 10.0 Incoming” (petecooper, 20 Oct 2026)
- PHP2Shell – official website – why does every vulnerability need a name, slogan, and website now?
- Wiz Research: “PHP2Shell: AI uncovers critical RCE vulnerabilities affecting 70% of the Internet” – these are one of the companies who found the bugs.
- PHP News Archive: “Upcoming Critical PHP Security Release” (20 Oct 2026) – how The PHP Group announced the vulnerability. Note the timelines.
- Wikipedia: PHP2Shell – not too detailed but at least they’re not trying to sell you anything.
- AWS Security Blog: “Amazon Threat Intelligence identifies PHP2Shell exploitation prior to public disclosure in MadPot” – they are trying to sell you something, but they’re still doing some interesting analysis.
eMudhra (CVE-2026-111943 for Golang response)
On the exact same day (20th October 2026), Mozilla announced that they were blocking 8 intermediate certificates signed by Indian certificate authority eMudhra. This happened after a pseudonymous security researcher known only as “Wayne” reported to several big tech firms (such as Mozilla, Apple, Google, Microsoft, etc.) that the certificate authority were using laughably poor quality private keys for their intermediate certificates. Where a secure key might be a 100 digit number, eMudhra were using keys like “115”, “56”, and “4”. They must’ve been following RFC 1149.5:
There are no indications that this was found or exploited using AI or LLMs, although researcher Scott Helme notes that given a single prompt, Claude was able to recover the private keys of the intermediate certs.
At the time of writing (23rd Oct), eMudhra has announced that it will be retiring from the certificate authority space. In unrelated news, a farmer has announced that he has shut his stable door, following reports of an escaped horse.
Links:
- Mozilla Security Blog: “Protecting Firefox users following the compromise of eMudhra intermediate certificates”
- Scott Helme: “Eight Bits of Trust; eMudhra’s CA keys cracked in milliseconds”
- eMudhra press release: “eMudhra to Exit global SSL/TLS Certificate Business”
- eMudhra Intermediate CA Compromise – research announcement and trust store checker
The next day, cloud provider Railway announced that they found evidence that hackers had accessed and even decrypted environment variables from their platform, which often hold secrets such as database credentials, API keys, etc. In their statement, they said that they believed that this was part of a concerted effort aimed at compromising companies that provide AI inference.
What would the end goal be here? At the time of writing (23rd Oct), we have very little information to go on. Is this “unauthorized third party” (official announcements of “some randos got into our computers” always find a way to make it seem like a terms of service agreement, maybe that way they think people won’t pay attention to it) trying to spy on people using AI inference to see what they’re doing, even stealing new models or research? Or maybe they’re trying to build a network of compromised inference providers for their own nefarious generative AI purposes (like finding more PHP bugs).
Links:
- Railway Blog: “Security Disclosure: Wednesday October 21st”
- Hacker News discussion of the Railway security disclosure
GitLab (CVE-2026-97229 and CVE-2026-110264)
On 12th October 2026, GitLab warned of a max severity bug in GitLab CI/CD’s regular expression parsing that could enable attackers to execute arbitrary code (another RCE) using a specially crafted regex. This is a CVSS score of 10.0 which is the maximum possible, meaning “this is pretty much as bad as they come”3. This was followed on 21st October 2026 by yet another regex integer overflow RCE, another 10.0.
This follows hot on the heels of yet another 10.0 CVSS CVE from last month (CVE-2026-85706), that time related to path traversal. All three of these bugs were reported through GitLab’s HackerOne bug bounty program. When it became clear that LLMs could research vulnerabilities and write exploits, there was a lot of talk about shutting down bug bounty programs because they didn’t make sense anymore. I’m sure GitLab are glad they didn’t do that now.
Although GitLab is used very widely across academia, government, and private companies, this doesn’t seem to have got as much attention. CVEs in GitLab are obviously very serious, especially for private companies, as a lot of their vitally important intellectual property is stored in there, and having that leak could be disastrous. Often, companies put their GitLab instance behind a VPN/firewall so that they aren’t publicly accessible, which greatly reduces the risk associated with this. It’s also not entirely clear whether these CVEs require specific conditions like publicly accessible projects, user self-registration, etc. It does seem like CVE-2026-110264 requires at least one public project, but I can’t find any information on the conditions around the earlier CVE.
There’s no indication that these were discovered using AI or LLMs. They may have been, but there’s no reason at this point to think they were.
Links:
On 21st October, a bug in musl’s libc related to regex (libc has regex? Apparently…) was announced that leads to denial of service at least, if not code execution. As far as I can tell, this is entirely coincidental in timing and not related to the GitLab bugs, which both also seem to be integer overflows when parsing untrusted regular expressions, one reported on the exact same day. Who knew a regex engine was such a security issue – is regex the new font rendering? The GitLab bugs were both found by a Swede called Johan Carlsson (joaxcar) while the musl bug was reported by Julien Voisin, a French self-proclaimed “open sourcerer”.
Links:
